category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: According to the WHO, Diabetes Mellitus is a heterogeneous group of diseases primarily characterized by a state of [___] hyperglycemia.
back:
• Chronic
• Resulting from defective insulin secretion or action
• Influenced by joint genetic and environmental etiologies
• Leads to multi-organ microvascular and macrovascular complications

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
coreConcept: WHO Fasting Plasma Glucose Diagnostic Threshold
front: A 50-year-old asymptomatic male presents for a check-up. His Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) is 130 mg/dl (7.2 mmol/l). Based on WHO diagnostic criteria, this finding indicates [___].
back:
• Diabetes Mellitus
• WHO threshold for FPG is ≥ 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l)
• Requires second abnormal test or clinical symptoms for diagnosis
• Differentiates from Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG)

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Explain the biological mechanism regarding insulin that constitutes the underlying cause of Diabetes Mellitus as defined by the WHO.
back:
• Defective insulin production (beta-cell failure)
• Impaired insulin action (peripheral resistance)
• Disruption of glucose, fat, and amino acid metabolism
• Results in prolonged, systemic hyperglycemia

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Contrast the WHO diagnostic thresholds for 'Impaired Glucose Tolerance' (IGT) with those of 'Impaired Fasting Glucose' (IFG) regarding 2-hour post-glucose load levels.
back:
• IGT: 2-h plasma glucose is 140–200 mg/dl (7.8–11.1 mmol/l)
• IFG: 2-h plasma glucose is < 140 mg/dl (< 7.8 mmol/l)
• Both represent intermediate 'at-risk' metabolic states

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Specify the standard parameters for conducting the Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) to meet WHO epidemiological survey requirements.
back:
• 75g anhydrous oral glucose load
• Measurement of venous plasma glucose
• Timing: Fasting sample and 2-hour post-ingestion sample
• Standard for defining IGT and DM

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
coreConcept: WHO Definition of Impaired Glucose Tolerance
front: Under the WHO clinical classification, the category described as a state intermediate between normality and diabetes, requiring an OGTT for definition, is [___].
back:
• Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT)
• Fasting glucose must be < 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l)
• Reflects an 'at-risk' group for progression to DM
• Clinically significant for preventing cardiovascular complications

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: According to the WHO clinical classification, diabetes diagnosed for the first time during pregnancy is categorized as [___].
back:
Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM).

*   Typically diagnosed via Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT).
*   Poses high risk to both mother and fetus.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: A 12-year-old child presents with abrupt polyuria, weight loss, and ketoacidosis. Identify the underlying pancreatic pathology.
back:
Immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic Beta-cells.

*   Leads to absolute insulin deficiency.
*   Associated with circulating insulin absence and elevated glucagon.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: How does the 2-hour plasma glucose level distinguish Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT) from Diabetes Mellitus?
back:
IGT: 140–200 mg/dl (7.8–11.1 mmol/l).
DM: ≥200 mg/dl (≥11.1 mmol/l).

*   IGT is an intermediate 'at-risk' state.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Contrast the clinical onset and ketosis tendency of Type 1 DM versus Type 2 DM.
back:
Type 1: Abrupt onset, rapid progression, high ketosis tendency.
Type 2: Gradual/silent onset, slow progression, resistant to ketosis.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Describe the physiological necessity of exogenous insulin in the management of Type 1 Diabetes.
back:
Required to reverse the catabolic state.

*   Prevents ketoacidosis.
*   Reduces hyperglucagonemia.
*   Maintains glucose, fat, and amino acid metabolism.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: To meet the diagnostic criteria for Diabetes Mellitus, the fasting plasma glucose must be ≥[___] mg/dl.
back:
126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l).

*   Must be confirmed by 2-hour post-glucose load test if uncertain.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: An obese patient presents with hyperglycemia, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. Identify this clinical cluster and its primary driver.
back:
Insulin Resistance Syndrome (Syndrome X).

*   Primary driver: Genetic defect producing insulin resistance.
*   Exacerbated by central/visceral obesity.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Differentiate the etiology of Malnutrition-Related Diabetes Mellitus (MRDM) from the secondary types of diabetes.
back:
MRDM: Partial Beta-cell failure due to early childhood PEM.
Secondary: Result of specific conditions (pancreatic disease, drug-induced, or hormonal abnormalities).

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Distinguish the role of HLA markers in the development of Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
Type 1: Strongly associated with HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4.
Type 2: No HLA association identified.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Identify the primary genetic markers associated with the highest risk of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4.

*   Risk is highest in individuals possessing both markers simultaneously.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: According to the WHO, Diabetes Mellitus is a heterogeneous group of diseases characterized by a state of [___].
back:
• Chronic hyperglycemia
• Results from diverse genetic and environmental etiologies acting jointly.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: A 45-year-old male presents for a routine check-up. His fasting plasma glucose is 132 mg/dl. Based on WHO diagnostic criteria, this finding indicates [___].
back:
• Diabetes Mellitus
• Threshold for diagnosis is fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l).

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Explain the role of the 2-hour Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) in defining the 'at-risk' state of Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT).
back:
• IGT is defined as fasting glucose < 7.0 mmol/l (126 mg/dl)
• AND 2-hour post-75g glucose load between 7.8 and 11.1 mmol/l (140–200 mg/dl).

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Contrast the WHO diagnostic thresholds for 'Impaired Fasting Glucose' (IFG) versus 'Diabetes Mellitus' using fasting plasma glucose values.
back:
• IFG: 110–125 mg/dl (6.1–6.9 mmol/l)
• Diabetes Mellitus: ≥ 126 mg/dl (≥ 7.0 mmol/l).

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Identify the metabolic hormone defect that serves as the underlying cause for the variable clinical manifestations of Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Defective production of insulin
• Defective action of insulin
• Affects glucose, fat, and amino acid metabolism.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: The WHO clinical classification of diabetes includes Type 1, Type 2, Gestational Diabetes, and [___] diabetes mellitus.
back:
• Malnutrition-related diabetes mellitus (MRDM)
• Other types secondary to pancreatic, hormonal, or drug-induced abnormalities.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: An asymptomatic 50-year-old obese female has a random blood sugar of 210 mg/dl. According to the WHO text, why is a 'standard oral glucose test' still preferred over random testing for epidemiological diagnosis?
back:
• Random blood sugar is unsatisfactory for epidemiological use
• OGTT (2-hour value) is the cornerstone for precise frequency estimates.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Describe the clinical presentation and insulin status that distinguishes Type 1 Diabetes from Type 2 in the untreated state.
back:
• Type 1: Abrupt onset, typically <30 years, insulin virtually absent, ketosis-prone
• Type 2: Gradual onset, middle-aged/elderly, slow to ketosis, insulin resistant.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Explain the progression from insulin resistance to hypertension within the context of 'Syndrome X' (Metabolic Syndrome).
back:
• Insulin resistance causes hyperinsulinemia
• Excess insulin increases sodium retention by renal tubules
• Leads to hypertension and stimulated endothelial proliferation.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Which specific biochemical test is recommended at half-yearly intervals to provide a long-term index (2–3 months) of glycemic control?
back:
• Glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
• Reflects mean blood glucose during the red cell lifetime.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: In Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, over 90 percent of cases are characterized by the immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic [___].
back:
Beta cells (̢ cells). 
- Leads to absolute insulin deficiency.
- Typically results in abrupt clinical onset.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: A 12-year-old boy presents with sudden weight loss, polyuria, and thirst. Labs reveal ketoacidosis and virtually absent circulating insulin. Identify the most likely WHO clinical classification.
back:
Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (IDDM).
- Common in children (highest in 10-14 years).
- Characterized by catabolic state and ketosis.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Explain how central obesity contributes to the pathophysiology of insulin resistance in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
Abdominal adiposity determines insulin resistance by:
- Reducing the number of insulin receptors on target cells.
- Altering the interaction between insulin and its receptors.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Contrast Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus based on their association with Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) markers.
back:
Type 1 DM: Strongly associated with HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4.
- Type 2 DM: Not HLA-associated.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Detail the metabolic components that constitute 'Syndrome X' (Insulin Resistance Syndrome) in obese patients.
back:
Hyperglycemia.
- Hyperinsulinemia.
- Dyslipidemia.
- Hypertension.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: The diagnostic state intermediate between normality and diabetes, defined by a 2-hour post-glucose load between 140-200 mg/dl, is [___].
back:
Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT).
- Considered an 'at-risk' group.
- Defined specifically by Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT).

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: A 30-year-old pregnant woman is found to have high blood sugar for the first time during a routine prenatal check-up. State the clinical classification of her condition.
back:
Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM).
- Diagnosed for the first time during pregnancy.
- Poses high risk to both mother and fetus.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Explain why Type 1 Diabetes is considered a more 'catabolic' disorder compared to Type 2 Diabetes regarding hormonal profile.
back:
Circulating insulin is virtually absent.
- Plasma glucagon is elevated.
- Beta cells fail to respond to insulinogenic stimuli.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Distinguish between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes regarding the typical age of onset and the speed of symptom progression.
back:
Type 1: Abrupt onset; usually <30 years.
- Type 2: Gradual onset; middle-aged or elderly.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Name the WHO clinical category of diabetes that specifically results from pancreatic disorders, hormonal abnormalities, or drug induction.
back:
Other types (Secondary Diabetes).
- Includes causes like cystic fibrosis or genetic mutations of the insulin gene.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: According to the WHO, Diabetes Mellitus is defined as a heterogeneous group of metabolic diseases characterized by a state of chronic [___].
back:
* Hyperglycemia
* Results from diversity of etiologies (genetic and environmental)
* Leads to long-term damage to eyes, kidneys, and nerves.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: A 45-year-old male undergoes a health check-up. His venous plasma glucose after an 8-hour fast is 130 mg/dl. Based on WHO criteria, this value is diagnostic of [___].
back:
* Diabetes Mellitus
* The WHO diagnostic threshold for Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) is ≥ 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l).

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Describe the fundamental hormonal defect that leads to the metabolic disturbances seen in Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
* Defective production of insulin
* Defective action of insulin (insulin resistance)
* Results in impaired metabolism of glucose, fats, and amino acids.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Contrast the WHO criteria for Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT) and Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) based on fasting plasma levels.
back:
* IFG: Fasting plasma glucose 110–125 mg/dl (6.1–6.9 mmol/l)
* IGT: Fasting plasma glucose < 126 mg/dl (< 7.0 mmol/l) with specific 2-hour elevations.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Specify the standard glucose load dose used in the Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) for diagnosing Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO recommendations.
back:
* 75 grams of anhydrous glucose
* Dissolved in water
* Plasma glucose is measured 2 hours after ingestion.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: In the WHO clinical classification, the form of diabetes characterized by an absolute insulin deficiency due to pancreatic beta-cell destruction is [___].
back:
* Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (IDDM)
* Typically abrupt onset
* Usually occurs in individuals < 30 years of age
* Ketosis-prone.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: A pregnant woman's glucose intolerance is first recognized during her second trimester. According to WHO classification, this condition is labeled as [___].
back:
* Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
* Poses high health risks to both mother and fetus
* Requires re-evaluation postpartum.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Explain the physiological basis for using Glycosylated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) as a long-term indicator of blood glucose control.
back:
* Glucose complexes with hemoglobin proportional to blood concentration
* Reflects mean glucose levels over the red cell lifespan
* Provides index for previous 2–3 months.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Differentiate Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus based on their typical clinical onset and ketosis tendency.
back:
* Type 1: Abrupt onset; prone to ketosis; absolute insulin lack
* Type 2: Gradual onset; slow to develop ketosis; relative insulin deficiency/resistance.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Identify the minimum 2-hour post-load (75g OGTT) venous plasma glucose level required to confirm a diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
* ≥ 200 mg/dl (11.1 mmol/l)
* Levels between 140–200 mg/dl indicate Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT).

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: According to WHO, Diabetes Mellitus is a heterogeneous group of diseases characterized by a state of chronic [___].
back:
• Hyperglycemia.
• It results from defective production or action of insulin.
• This affects glucose, fat, and amino acid metabolism.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: A 12-year-old child presents with abrupt weight loss, polyuria, and ketoacidosis. If this condition is immune-mediated, the underlying pathophysiology involves the destruction of [___].
back:
• Pancreatic Beta cells.
• Occurs in over 90% of Type 1 cases.
• Leads to absolute insulin deficiency and a catabolic state.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Explain the physiological link between insulin resistance and hypertension in metabolic Syndrome X.
back:
• Hyperinsulinemia increases renal sodium retention.
• High insulin levels stimulate endothelial proliferation.
• This initiates atherosclerosis and increases blood pressure.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Contrast the WHO laboratory criteria for Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT) versus Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG).
back:
• IGT: 2-hour glucose is 140–200 mg/dl (7.8–11.1 mmol/l).
• IFG: Fasting glucose is 110–125 mg/dl (6.1–6.9 mmol/l).
• IGT identifies an intermediate 'at-risk' group.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Identify the characteristic clinical onset and typical patient profile for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Onset: Gradual and often discovered by chance.
• Population: Mainly middle-aged and elderly individuals.
• Linked with obesity and sedentary lifestyles.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: The WHO threshold for diagnosing Diabetes Mellitus using a fasting plasma glucose level is [___] mg/dl or higher.
back:
• 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l).
• Fasting must be assured for accurate diagnosis.
• Measured in venous plasma for standardized results.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: A patient has a random blood sugar of 160 mg/dl, but you suspect poor control over the last 3 months. The most appropriate laboratory index to confirm this is [___].
back:
• Glycosylated Haemoglobin (HbA1c).
• Reflects mean glucose over the red cell life-time.
• Provides a long-term index of glycemic control.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Describe the metabolic state of untreated Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus regarding insulin and glucagon levels.
back:
• Insulin: Virtually absent circulating levels.
• Glucagon: Elevated plasma levels (hyperglucagonemia).
• Results in unchecked gluconeogenesis and ketosis.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Distinguish between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes regarding age of onset and ketosis tendency.
back:
• Type 1: Typically <30 years; high ketosis tendency.
• Type 2: Middle-aged/elderly; slow to ketosis.
• Type 1 is lethal without exogenous insulin.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: State the WHO 2-hour plasma glucose value required to diagnose Diabetes Mellitus following a 75g oral glucose load.
back:
• 200 mg/dl (11.1 mmol/l) or greater.
• Standardized via the Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT).
• Venous plasma is the required sample type.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is primarily an immune-mediated disorder where the destruction of [___] leads to an absolute deficiency of insulin.
back:
• Pancreatic Beta (β) cells.
• Results in absolute insulin deficiency.
• Usually leads to ketosis in its untreated state.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: A 12-year-old child presents with sudden onset polyuria, weight loss, and ketonuria. Lab results show a random blood glucose of 300 mg/dl. Identify the most likely clinical classification.
back:
• Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (IDDM).
• Characterized by abrupt onset and catabolic state.
• Requires exogenous insulin for survival.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Explain the biological function of the hyperinsulinemia observed in Syndrome X (Insulin Resistance Syndrome).
back:
• Compensates for peripheral insulin resistance.
• Attempt to correct hyperglycemia.
• Excessive levels contribute to triglyceride rise and sodium retention (hypertension).

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Contrast the typical age of onset and ketosis tendency between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Type 1: Typically <30 years; abrupt onset; high ketosis tendency.
• Type 2: Middle-aged/Elderly; gradual onset; slow to ketosis.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Define the diagnostic status of 'Impaired Glucose Tolerance' (IGT) based on the 2-hour post-glucose load values.
back:
• Intermediate state between normality and diabetes.
• 2-hour plasma glucose: 140 mg/dl to 200 mg/dl (7.8–11.1 mmol/l).
• Fasting plasma glucose must be <126 mg/dl.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: The specific type of diabetes often diagnosed for the first time during pregnancy is known as [___].
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM).
• Poses risks to both mother and fetus.
• Requires screening during pregnancy.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: A young patient in a developing region presents with diabetes and a history of severe childhood protein-energy malnutrition. Name this specific clinical classification.
back:
• Malnutrition-Related Diabetes Mellitus (MRDM).
• Common in young people in developing societies.
• Result of partial failure of Beta-cell function due to PEM.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Describe the genetic association of Human Leukocyte Antigens (HLA) with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus susceptibility.
back:
• Strongly associated with HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4.
• Highest risk in individuals with both DR3 and DR4.
• Type 2 DM has no HLA association.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Distinguish 'Impaired Fasting Glucose' (IFG) from 'Impaired Glucose Tolerance' (IGT) based on the primary blood glucose abnormality.
back:
• IFG: Elevated fasting glucose (110–125 mg/dl) with normal 2-hr glucose.
• IGT: Elevated 2-hr post-load glucose (140–200 mg/dl) with non-diabetic fasting levels.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: List three distinct etiologies classified under 'Other types' of secondary Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Pancreatic disorders (e.g., cystic fibrosis, pancreatitis).
• Hormonal abnormalities (e.g., acromegaly).
• Drug-induced (e.g., corticosteroids).

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: According to WHO criteria, Diabetes Mellitus is defined by a Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) level greater than or equal to [___] mg/dl.
back:
• 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l).
• Measured in venous plasma.
• Requires confirmation on a second occasion if the patient is asymptomatic.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: A 45-year-old asymptomatic male undergoes screening. His fasting plasma glucose is 120 mg/dl and his 2-hour post 75g oral glucose load is 180 mg/dl. Identify his glycemic status.
back:
• Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT).
• FPG is < 126 mg/dl (not diabetic).
• 2-hour glucose is between 140–200 mg/dl.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Describe the core underlying pathophysiology of Diabetes Mellitus as defined by the WHO.
back:
• A heterogeneous group of diseases.
• Characterized by chronic hyperglycemia.
• Results from defective insulin secretion, defective insulin action, or both.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: A patient presents with a fasting plasma glucose of 115 mg/dl and a 2-hour OGTT value of 130 mg/dl. Contrast this status with the diagnostic threshold for Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Patient has Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG).
• IFG: FPG 110–125 mg/dl.
• DM: FPG ≥ 126 mg/dl or 2-hr OGTT ≥ 200 mg/dl.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Outline the standard procedure for the Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) used for WHO diagnostic purposes.
back:
• 75g anhydrous glucose load.
• Dissolved in water and taken orally.
• Venous plasma glucose measured 2 hours later.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: For the diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus, the WHO recommends a 2-hour plasma glucose value of [___] mmol/l or higher following a 75g oral glucose load.
back:
• 11.1 mmol/l.
• Equivalent to 200 mg/dl.
• Used for diagnosis even if fasting levels are normal.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: A pregnant woman is screened for glucose intolerance during her 24th week of gestation. If she meets the criteria for hyperglycemia for the first time, name the WHO clinical classification category.
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM).
• Carbohydrate intolerance with onset or first recognition during pregnancy.
• Poses high health risks to both mother and fetus.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Identify the primary clinical differences between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus regarding onset and insulin levels.
back:
• Type 1: Abrupt onset, < 30 years, virtually absent insulin, ketosis-prone.
• Type 2: Gradual onset, middle-aged/elderly, partial insulin deficiency or resistance, slow to ketosis.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Distinguish between the diagnostic criteria for Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT) and Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG).
back:
• IGT: 2-hr glucose 140–200 mg/dl (7.8–11.1 mmol/l).
• IFG: Fasting glucose 110–125 mg/dl (6.1–6.9 mmol/l).
• Both represent intermediate 'at-risk' states.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: List the high-risk groups prioritizing WHO-recommended screening for Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Age ≥ 40 years.
• Obese individuals and those with family history.
• Women with history of babies > 4.5kg.
• Patients with premature atherosclerosis.

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: According to WHO, Diabetes Mellitus is defined as a heterogeneous group of diseases characterized by a state of chronic [___].
back:
- Hyperglycemia
- Results from diverse aetiologies (genetic and environmental)

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: A 45-year-old male presents with a fasting plasma glucose of 130 mg/dl on two occasions. State the underlying diagnosis based on WHO diagnostic thresholds.
back:
- Diabetes Mellitus
- Threshold for diagnosis is ≥ 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l)

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Explain the primary physiological defect that leads to the metabolic abnormalities in Diabetes Mellitus as defined by the WHO.
back:
- Defective production of insulin
- Defective action of insulin
- Affects glucose, fat, and amino acid metabolism

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Contrast the components of Insulin Resistance Syndrome (Syndrome X) with the criteria for overt Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
- Syndrome X: Hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinaemia, dyslipidaemia, and hypertension
- Overt DM: Specifically defined by glucose thresholds (Fasting ≥126 mg/dl; 2-hr ≥200 mg/dl)

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: List the three main clinical categories in the WHO classification of diabetes and related abnormalities of glucose tolerance.
back:
- Diabetes Mellitus (DM)
- Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT)
- Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: To diagnose Diabetes Mellitus using the 2-hour venous plasma glucose test after a 75g load, the value must be greater than or equal to [___] mg/dl.
back: - 200 mg/dl (11.1 mmol/l)

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: A patient’s laboratory results show a fasting plasma glucose of 115 mg/dl. Provide the specific WHO term for this intermediate state of hyperglycemia.
back:
- Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG)
- Criteria: 110 mg/dl to 125 mg/dl (6.1 to 6.9 mmol/l)

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
coreConcept: Differential Diagnosis of IGT vs IFG
front: Explain why a patient with a fasting glucose of 115 mg/dl but a 2-hour post-load glucose of 160 mg/dl is classified as having IGT rather than IFG.
back:
- IFG requires 2-hour glucose < 140 mg/dl
- 160 mg/dl falls in the 140–200 mg/dl range, which defines Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT)

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
coreConcept: Comparison of Type 1 vs Type 2 DM
front: Distinguish between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus regarding their metabolic nature and typical age of onset.
back:
- Type 1: Age < 30; abrupt onset; insulin absent; ketosis-prone
- Type 2: Middle-aged/elderly; gradual onset; insulin resistance or partial deficiency

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Name the specific glucose load (in grams) used in the 'standard oral glucose test' recommended by the WHO for diagnosing DM.
back: - 75 grams of oral glucose

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: According to the WHO definition, Diabetes Mellitus is a heterogeneous group of metabolic diseases characterized by a state of chronic [___].
back:
- Hyperglycemia
- Results from defective insulin production or action
- Associated with long-term multi-organ complications

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: An asymptomatic 50-year-old male has a fasting plasma glucose of 130 mg/dl. Identify the diagnosis based on WHO diagnostic thresholds.
back:
- Diabetes Mellitus
- Threshold is ≥ 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l)
- Requires confirmation on a subsequent day

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Explain how the defective action of insulin leads to the metabolic disturbances seen in Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
- Impairs glucose utilization
- Disturbs fat and amino acid metabolism
- Causes hyperglycemia and glycosuria

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Contrast the WHO biochemical thresholds for Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT) versus Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG).
back:
- IGT: 2-h glucose 140–200 mg/dl
- IFG: Fasting glucose 110–125 mg/dl
- Both indicate intermediate risk for diabetes

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Enumerate the four main clinical categories included in the WHO classification of Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
- Type 1 (IDDM)
- Type 2 (NIDDM)
- Malnutrition-related (MRDM)
- Other types (secondary causes)

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: To satisfy WHO criteria via an Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT), the 2-hour plasma glucose must be greater than or equal to [___] mg/dl.
back:
- 200 mg/dl
- Equivalent to 11.1 mmol/l
- Measured after a 75g glucose load

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: An obese patient presents with hypertension, high triglycerides, and hyperinsulinemia. Name this condition according to the provided text.
back:
- Insulin Resistance Syndrome (Syndrome X)
- Driven by genetic defects and obesity
- High insulin stimulates atherosclerosis

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Describe the physiological hallmarks that distinguish the catabolic state of untreated Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
- Virtually absent circulating insulin
- Elevated plasma glucagon
- Beta cells fail to respond to stimuli

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Contrast the typical age of onset and progression rate between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
- Type 1: Abrupt onset; <30 years; ketosis-prone
- Type 2: Gradual onset; middle-aged/elderly; slow to ketosis

category: Define Diabetes Mellitus according to WHO (World Health Organization) criteria
front: Identify the standard oral glucose load required to perform a diagnostic OGTT as recommended by the WHO.
back:
- 75 grams
- Administered as anhydrous glucose
- Baseline for 2-hour plasma testing

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: WHO classification of Diabetes Mellitus includes Type 1, Type 2, Other types, and [___], a category specifically associated with protein-energy malnutrition in young individuals.
back:
• Malnutrition-related diabetes mellitus (MRDM)
• Linked to partial β-cell failure from childhood protein-energy malnutrition
• Common in developing countries like Pakistan
• Often affects lean young adults

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: A 12-year-old child presents with abrupt onset polyuria, weight loss, and ketosis. The underlying pathophysiology involves over 90% of cases being [___] resulting in absolute insulin deficiency.
back:
• Immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic β-cells
• Associated with HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 markers
• Results in absolute absence of circulating insulin
• Characterized by hyperglucagonemia and a catabolic state

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Explain the role of central adiposity in the development of Syndrome X (Insulin Resistance Syndrome).
back:
• Promotes insulin resistance, the core defect
• Reduces the number of insulin receptors on target cells
• Triggers hyperinsulinemia, leading to triglyceride elevation and renal sodium retention
• Stimulates endothelial proliferation initiating atherosclerosis

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Distinguish between Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT) and Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) based on WHO diagnostic plasma glucose levels.
back:
• IGT: Fasting <126 mg/dl AND 2-hr post-load 140–200 mg/dl
• IFG: Fasting 110–125 mg/dl AND 2-hr post-load (if measured) <140 mg/dl
• IGT is defined strictly by the Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT)

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Identify the environmental risk factors that typically 'unmask' susceptibility to Type 2 Diabetes in genetically vulnerable Asians.
back:
• Sedentary lifestyle and lack of physical exercise
• Diets high in saturated fats and low in fiber
• Urbanization and unfavorable lifestyle modifications
• Central obesity (waist-to-hip ratio is a stronger determinant than BMI)

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: According to WHO, Diabetes Mellitus is diagnosed when the fasting plasma glucose is ≥[___] mg/dl.
back:
• 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l)
• Alternatively, 2-hour post-load glucose ≥200 mg/dl (11.1 mmol/l)
• Based on venous plasma glucose measurements
• Cornerstone of epidemiological surveys and diagnosis

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: In Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, the immune-mediated destruction specifically targets the [___] cells of the pancreas.
back:
Pancreatic Beta (̢β) cells.
- Results in absolute insulin deficiency.
- Circulating insulin is virtually absent.
- Over 90% of cases are immune-mediated.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: A 12-year-old child presents with sudden onset polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss. Lab tests show elevated plasma glucagon and ketosis. Identify the specific subtype of diabetes.
back:
Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (Insulin-dependent).
- Typical abrupt onset in individuals < 30 years.
- Characterized by ketosis-prone states.
- Pancreatic β-cells fail to respond to insulinogenic stimuli.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Explain the role of excessive insulin in the development of hypertension within the Insulin Resistance Syndrome (Syndrome X).
back:
Excessive insulin levels contribute to:
- Increased sodium retention by renal tubules.
- Induction of high triglyceride levels.
- Stimulation of endothelial proliferation causing atherosclerosis.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Contrast the onset and ketosis tendency between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
Type 1: Abrupt onset; ketosis-prone (lethal without insulin).
- Type 2: Gradual onset; slow to ketosis (compatible with long survival).
- Type 1 is catabolic; Type 2 is often associated with obesity.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: List the categories that fall under 'Other Types' of diabetes as per the WHO clinical classification.
back:
Secondary to:
- Pancreatic disorders (e.g., inflammation, neoplasm, cystic fibrosis).
- Hormonal abnormalities.
- Drug-induced or chemical-induced.
- Genetic defects of the insulin gene.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: According to WHO criteria, a diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus is confirmed if the 2-hour plasma glucose after a 75g oral glucose load is ≥ [___] mg/dl.
back:
200 mg/dl (11.1 mmol/l).
- Fasting plasma glucose must be ≥ 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l).
- Values between 140-200 mg/dl indicate Impaired Glucose Tolerance.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: A 28-year-old pregnant woman in her 26th week of gestation shows hyperglycemia for the first time during a routine check-up. State the classification and potential risks.
back:
Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM).
- Diagnosed for the first time during pregnancy.
- Risks: Intrauterine growth retardation, fetal macrosomia, and childhood obesity.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Describe the proposed mechanism of Malnutrition-related Diabetes Mellitus (MRDM) in young individuals.
back:
Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM) in early childhood causes:
- Partial failure of β-cell function.
- Impaired carbohydrate tolerance.
- Potential toxicity from cyanide-producing foods like cassava.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Distinguish between Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT) and Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) based on fasting plasma glucose levels.
back:
IFG: Fasting plasma glucose 110–125 mg/dl.
- IGT: Fasting plasma glucose < 126 mg/dl PLUS 2-hr PG 140–200 mg/dl.
- Both represent intermediate 'at-risk' states.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Identify the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) markers most strongly associated with the genetic risk of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4.
- Also associated with HLA-B8 and B15.
- Type 2 DM is not HLA-associated.
- 50% concordance in identical twins for Type 1.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: In the epide m iol o gy of Diabetes Mellitus, the specific ge ne tic markers associated with the highest risk for Type 1 Diabetes are [___].
back:
- Individuals possessing both HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4.
- Also associated with HLA-B8 and B15.
- These markers are not associated with Type 2 Diabetes.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
coreConcept: Central obesity vs BMI in DM risk
front: An overweight male presents with an increased waist-to-hip ratio. Explain the epidemiological significance of this specific fat distribution regarding Type 2 Diabetes risk.
back:
- Central/abdominal adiposity is a more powerful determinant of risk than BMI.
- It is a key driver of insulin resistance.
- High waist circumference correlates with adult weight gain risk.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Explain how a sedentary lifestyle acts as an environmental risk factor for the development of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
- Lack of physical activity alters the interaction between insulin and its receptors.
- It leads to decreased insulin sensitivity.
- Promotes the progression from impaired glucose tolerance to overt diabetes.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Contrast the genetic concordance rates and primary environmental 'triggers' between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
- Type 1: 50% twin concordance; triggered by viruses (Rubella, Mumps, Coxsackie B4).
- Type 2: 90% twin concordance; triggered by lifestyle (obesity, diet, inactivity).

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Outline the role of maternal diabetes as a host factor for the offspring's future metabolic health.
back:
- Offspring have a three-fold higher risk of diabetes than those born before the mother developed DM.
- Associated with high birth weight and childhood obesity.
- Linked to early-onset Type 2 Diabetes.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: The 'iceberg' phenomenon in diabetes epidemiology suggests that the submerged portion of the iceberg represents [___].
back:
- Undiagnosed asymptomatic cases.
- Individuals with impaired glucose tolerance (IGT).
- Cases that remain undetected due to inadequate screening.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
coreConcept: Urbanization as a DM risk factor
front: A population survey shows that diabetes prevalence is twice as high in urban areas compared to rural sectors. Attribute this finding to specific epidemiological risk factors.
back:
- Unfavourable modifications in lifestyle.
- Dietary shifts (high saturated fat, low fiber).
- Increased physical inactivity associated with urbanization.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
coreConcept: Dietary fat quality in DM risk
front: How does the quality of dietary fat intake influence the metabolic risk loop for Type 2 Diabetes?
back:
- Saturated fats: Reduce insulin sensitivity and increase fasting glucose.
- Unsaturated fats (vegetable/polyunsaturated): Improve glucose tolerance.
- High total fat (>37% energy) negates the benefits of fat quality.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Distinguish between the target age groups and onset characteristics of Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
- Type 1: Primarily children/adolescents (peak 10–14 years); abrupt onset.
- Type 2: Middle-aged and elderly; gradual onset, often discovered by chance.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Summarize the changing epidemiological trend of Diabetes regarding social class over the last 50 years.
back:
- Past: Higher prevalence in upper social classes.
- Present: More common in lower social classes.
- Shift is due to rapid lifestyle changes in lower socioeconomic groups.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is fundamentally characterized by the selective immune-mediated destruction of [___] in the islets of Langerhans.
back: Pancreatic beta cells. This results in an absolute insulin deficiency and is seen in over 90% of Type 1 cases.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
coreConcept: Clinical presentation and HLA association of Type 1 DM
front: A 12-year-old child presents with abrupt onset weight loss, polyuria, and ketoacidosis. Genetic testing shows HLA-DR3 and DR4 positivity. State the most likely clinical classification.
back: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (IDDM). Key indicators: abrupt childhood onset, propensity for ketoacidosis, and strong association with HLA-DR3/DR4 markers.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Explain the role of insulin resistance and beta-cell function in the development of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back: Type 2 DM involves a combination of peripheral insulin resistance and a relative (rather than absolute) insulin deficiency. The beta cells fail to compensate for the resistance over time.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Contrast Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus regarding their association with obesity and ketosis.
back: Type 1: Usually not associated with obesity; highly prone to ketosis. Type 2: Frequently associated with central obesity; generally slow to develop ketosis.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Identify the four clinical components that define Insulin Resistance Syndrome (Syndrome X).
back: 1. Hyperglycemia. 2. Hyperinsulinemia. 3. Dyslipidemia (high triglycerides). 4. Hypertension. Often exacerbated by abdominal obesity.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: The state characterized by a 2-hour plasma glucose value between 140 mg/dl and 200 mg/dl following a 75g oral glucose load is defined as [___].
back: Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT). This is an intermediate 'at-risk' category between normal glucose levels and clinical diabetes.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: A 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with hyperglycemia for the first time during her second trimester. Name the specific clinical classification for this condition.
back: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM). It poses risks to both mother and fetus, including intrauterine growth issues and neonatal complications.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Outline the diverse etiologies categorized under 'Other Types' of secondary diabetes mellitus.
back: Includes: 1. Pancreatic disorders (pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis). 2. Hormonal (Acromegaly, Cushing’s). 3. Drug-induced (Corticosteroids). 4. Genetic defects of insulin action.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Distinguish Malnutrition-Related Diabetes Mellitus (MRDM) from the two classic types regarding its target demographic and etiology.
back: MRDM affects young people in developing countries. It is linked to early childhood protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) and partial failure of beta-cell function.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Name the specific HLA markers associated with the highest risk for developing Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.
back: HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4. Individuals possessing both markers carry the highest genetic risk for the immune-mediated form of the disease.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: In the clinical classification of Diabetes Mellitus, the specific type associated with protein-energy malnutrition in early childhood is [___].
back:
• Malnutrition-related diabetes mellitus (MRDM).
• Caused by partial failure of beta-cell function due to early-life nutritional deficiency.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old male with central obesity presents with hypertension and dyslipidemia. Explain the proposed mechanism of endothelial proliferation in this 'Syndrome X' presentation.
back:
• Chronic hyperinsulinemia resulting from insulin resistance.
• High insulin levels directly stimulate endothelial cell proliferation, initiating the process of atherosclerosis.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Outline why the 2-hour value after a 75g oral glucose load is preferred over random blood sugar for epidemiological surveys.
back:
• Random blood samples only provide crude frequency estimates.
• The 2-hour OGTT is the 'cornerstone' of diagnosis for epidemiological accuracy and standardizing impaired glucose tolerance.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Distinguish between the genetic markers associated with Type 1 Diabetes versus the genetic associations found in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Type 1: Strong association with HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4.
• Type 2: No HLA association; characterized by high identical twin concordance (approx. 90%).

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Name the specific preventive strategy and primary drug used to reduce the incidence of Type 2 Diabetes in high-risk individuals by approximately 25-31%.
back:
• High-risk strategy.
• Metformin administration.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: According to WHO diagnostic criteria, 'Impaired Fasting Glucose' (IFG) is defined by a fasting plasma glucose level ranging from [___] mg/dl.
back:
• 110 mg/dl to 125 mg/dl (6.1 to 6.9 mmol/l).
• Requires a 2-hour plasma glucose of <140 mg/dl to confirm status.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: An obese pregnant woman gives birth to a neonate weighing 4.6 kg. Describe the subsequent epidemiological risk for both mother and child.
back:
• Mother: High risk for developing permanent Type 2 Diabetes.
• Child: High risk of childhood obesity and early-onset Type 2 Diabetes.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Differentiate the role of central adiposity (waist-to-hip ratio) from Body Mass Index (BMI) in predicting Type 2 Diabetes risk.
back:
• Central/visceral adiposity is a more powerful determinant than BMI.
• It is the primary driver of insulin resistance in Type 2 Diabetes pathogenesis.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Compare the metabolic effects of high saturated fat intake versus high intake of Non-Starch Polysaccharides (NSP) on insulin sensitivity.
back:
• Saturated Fats: Associated with higher fasting glucose and lower insulin sensitivity.
• NSP (Fiber): Protective; reduces blood glucose and insulin levels; minimum 20g/day recommended.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: List three environmental chemical agents known to be specifically toxic to pancreatic beta cells.
back:
• Alloxan.
• Streptozotocin.
• Rodenticide VALCOR.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is most strongly associated with the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) markers [___] and [___].
back:
• HLA-DR3
• HLA-DR4
• Individuals carrying both markers have the highest risk.
• These markers suggest an immune-mediated pathophysiology.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old obese male presents with hyperglycemia, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. Identify this clinical cluster and its underlying genetic-environmental defect.
back:
• Insulin Resistance Syndrome (Syndrome X)
• Pathophysiology: Genetic defect producing insulin resistance, exaggerated by obesity.
• Results in hyperinsulinemia, leading to atherosclerosis and hypertension.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
coreConcept: Obesity as a Diabetes Risk Factor
front: Explain how central adiposity functions as a host risk factor for the development of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Central obesity (visceral fat) is a powerful determinant of insulin resistance.
• It reduces the number of insulin receptors on target cells.
• BMI and waist-to-hip ratio are key longitudinal risk predictors.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Contrast the genetic concordance of Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes using monozygotic twin studies.
back:
• Type 1 DM: ~50% concordance (lower genetic influence).
• Type 2 DM: ~90% concordance (very strong genetic component).
• Type 2 is not HLA-associated, unlike Type 1.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Identify the 'probable' dietary risk factors that increase the susceptibility to Type 2 Diabetes according to epidemiological evidence.
back:
• High saturated fat intake.
• Low intake of non-starch polysaccharides (dietary fiber).
• Total fat intake exceeding 37% of total energy.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: In the epidemiological 'iceberg' of diabetes, the submerged portion represents [___] cases in the community.
back:
• Undiagnosed or asymptomatic cases.
• Type 2 DM is often discovered by chance due to gradual onset.
• Highlights the failure of routine detection in primary care.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: A child is born with low birth weight but undergoes rapid growth catch-up. Predict the future risk for metabolic disease in this child.
back:
• High risk of subsequent Type 2 Diabetes.
• Intrauterine growth retardation followed by rapid catch-up is a significant host factor.
• Maternal diabetes increases offspring risk three-fold.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: How do environmental 'triggers' like viral infections lead to the onset of Type 1 Diabetes in susceptible hosts?
back:
• Viruses (Rubella, Mumps, Coxsackie B4) trigger immune-mediated B-cell destruction.
• Occurs in genetically predisposed individuals (HLA-DR3/DR4).
• Results in absolute insulin deficiency and abrupt clinical onset.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Distinguish between the primary prevention 'Population Strategy' and 'High-Risk Strategy' for Diabetes.
back:
• Population Strategy: Primordial prevention; promoting healthy nutrition and physical activity for the whole community.
• High-Risk Strategy: Targeted screening and lifestyle correction for the obese, elderly, or those with family history.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Identify the most common age group for the highest incidence of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• 10–14 years of age.
• Typically occurs in individuals less than 30 years old.
• Onset is abrupt and associated with ketosis if untreated.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: In Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, the pancreatic [___] fail to respond to all insulinogenic stimuli, resulting in a virtually complete absence of circulating insulin.
back:
Beta (β) cells.
• Results in absolute insulin deficiency.
• Leads to a catabolic state with elevated glucagon.
• Typically abrupt onset in individuals <30 years.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: A 12-year-old presents with abrupt weight loss, polyuria, and ketoacidosis. Which pathophysiological mechanism is responsible for this presentation according to the classification?
back:
Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (IDDM).
• Immune-mediated destruction (>90% cases).
• Absolute insulin deficiency.
• Ketosis-prone untreated state.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Explain the role of excessive insulin levels in contributing to hypertension within the context of Syndrome X (Insulin Resistance Syndrome).
back:
• Increases sodium retention by renal tubules.
• Stimulates endothelial proliferation.
• Promotes atherosclerosis and vascular resistance.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Contrast Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes regarding their genetic associations with HLA markers and twin concordance rates.
back:
• Type 1: Strong HLA-DR3/DR4 association; 50% twin concordance.
• Type 2: No HLA association; ~90% twin concordance (stronger genetic component).

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Describe the clinical features and etiology of Malnutrition-related Diabetes Mellitus (MRDM).
back:
• Affects young people in developing regions.
• Partial failure of beta-cell function due to PEM (Kwashiorkor).
• Included in WHO clinical classification.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: The metabolic state intermediate between normality and diabetes, defined by a 2-hour post-glucose load between 140mg/dl and 200mg/dl, is known as [___].
back:
Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT).
• Fasting plasma glucose must be <126 mg/dl.
• Considered a high-risk 'iceberg' group for future DM.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: A 28-year-old female is diagnosed with hyperglycemia for the first time during her 24th week of pregnancy. What is the clinical classification of this condition?
back:
Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM).
• Diagnosed first during pregnancy.
• Increases risks for mother and fetus (e.g., macrosomia).

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Differentiate between the insulin status and ketosis tendency in Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Type 1: Absolute insulin deficiency; ketosis-prone (lethal without treatment).
• Type 2: Relative insulin deficiency/resistance; slow to ketosis; compatible with long survival.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: Outline the biological loop in Syndrome X where obesity leads to coronary artery disease.
back: Obesity → Insulin resistance → Hyperglycemia → Hyperinsulinemia → Endothelial proliferation/dyslipidemia → Atherosclerosis → Coronary artery disease.

category: Classify types of Diabetes Mellitus
front: List three specific causes of 'Other types' of secondary diabetes according to the clinical classification.
back:
• Pancreatic disorders (e.g., pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis).
• Hormonal abnormalities.
• Drug-induced (e.g., corticosteroids).
• Genetic mutations of the insulin gene.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: In Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, the strongest genetic susceptibility is associated with the human leukocyte antigens [___] and [___].
back:
• HLA-DR3
• HLA-DR4
• Individuals carrying both DR3 and DR4 alleles have the highest risk of immune-mediated beta-cell destruction.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: An obese 45-year-old male presents with hypertension, high triglycerides, and elevated fasting glucose. Explain the pathophysiological link between his central adiposity and insulin resistance.
back:
• Central obesity reduces the number of insulin receptors on target cells.
• Visceral fat increases free fatty acid levels, impairing glucose uptake.
• Chronic hyperglycemia leads to compensatory hyperinsulinemia and vascular atherosclerosis.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Outline the mechanism by which early childhood protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) acts as an epidemiological risk factor for adult-onset diabetes.
back:
• Malnutrition in infancy (Kwashiorkor) results in partial failure of pancreatic beta-cell function.
• Leads to permanent impairment of carbohydrate tolerance.
• Classified specifically as Malnutrition-Related Diabetes Mellitus (MRDM).

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Contrast the genetic concordance between identical twins and the primary HLA association for Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Concordance: ~90% in Type 2 (stronger genetic link) versus ~50% in Type 1.
• HLA Association: Type 1 is strongly HLA-associated (DR3/DR4), while Type 2 has no HLA association.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Identify the specific dietary modifications that epidemiological studies demonstrate as protective against the progression from impaired glucose tolerance to Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Minimum daily intake of 20 grams of dietary fiber (NSP).
• Replacement of saturated fats with monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids.
• Consumption of low-glycemic index foods and whole grains.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: The risk of Type 2 Diabetes is more accurately determined by [___] or [___] than by Body Mass Index (BMI) alone.
back:
• Waist circumference
• Waist-to-hip ratio
• These markers reflect central/visceral adiposity, which is the primary driver of insulin resistance.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
coreConcept: Maternal Risk Factors and Offspring Health
front: A woman with a history of gestational diabetes gives birth to a 4.6 kg infant. Describe the long-term epidemiological risks for the offspring.
back:
• High risk of developing childhood obesity.
• Three-fold increased risk of developing Type 2 Diabetes at an early age.
• Increased susceptibility if intrauterine growth retardation was followed by rapid weight catch-up.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Analyze the role of viral infections as 'environmental triggers' for Type 1 Diabetes in immunogenetically susceptible populations.
back:
• Implicated viruses include Mumps, Rubella, and Human Coxsackie Virus B4.
• Viruses trigger an autoimmune sequence in HLA-susceptible individuals.
• Results in progressive and absolute destruction of pancreatic beta cells.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Distinguish between the 'Population Strategy' and 'High-risk Strategy' regarding primary prevention of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Population Strategy: Primordial prevention focusing on community-wide healthy nutrition and physical activity.
• High-risk Strategy: Targets specific individuals (obese, sedentary, or family history) for intensive weight loss and diabetogenic drug avoidance.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Name the specific high-risk groups that should be prioritized for targeted screening using the 2-hour 75g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT).
back:
• Adults aged 40 years and older.
• Obese individuals and those with positive family history.
• Women who delivered babies >4.5 kg.
• Patients with premature atherosclerosis.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: In the context of genetic susceptibility, Type 1 Diabetes is most strongly associated with the [___] and DR4 alleles of the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) system.
back:
● HLA-DR3.
● Highest risk is carried by individuals with both DR3 and DR4.
● Type 1 is immune-mediated in over 90% of cases.
● Type 2 is not HLA-associated.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: A 12-year-old child presents with abrupt polyuria, weight loss, and ketosis. Lab tests show virtually absent circulating insulin. Identify the most likely classification and its peak incidence age.
back:
● Type 1 Diabetes (IDDM).
● Peak incidence: 10–14 years.
● Pathophysiology: Immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic β-cells.
● Clinical hallmark: Sudden onset and prone to ketosis.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Explain the physiological mechanism by which central obesity contributes to the development of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
● Insulin Resistance.
● Visceral adiposity reduces the number of insulin receptors on target cells.
● Causes decreased insulin sensitivity in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.
● Often results in compensatory hyperinsulinemia.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Contrast the genetic concordance of Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes as demonstrated in identical twin studies.
back:
● Type 2: ~90% concordance (strong genetic component).
● Type 1: ~50% concordance (suggests environmental triggers).
● Environmental factors are required to unmask genetic vulnerability in Type 1.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: List the specific dietary risk factors that are 'convincingly' associated with an increased risk of developing Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
● Overweight and obesity.
● Abdominal (central) adiposity.
● Physical inactivity.
● High intake of saturated fats and total fat (probable/possible).

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Urbanization is a significant environmental determinant; studies indicate the prevalence of diabetes is approximately [___] times higher in urban areas than in rural populations.
back:
● Twice (2x).
● Driven by sedentary lifestyles and dietary transitions.
● Linked to rapid economic transition in developing countries.
● Associated with increased intake of refined foods.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: A woman with a history of gestational diabetes gives birth to a baby weighing 4.6 kg. Describe the long-term metabolic risk for this offspring.
back:
● High risk of Type 2 Diabetes.
● Offspring often develop childhood obesity.
● Risk is three-fold higher if born after maternal diabetes onset.
● Linked to intrauterine growth environments.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Describe how a sedentary lifestyle facilitates the onset of Type 2 Diabetes at the cellular level.
back:
● Receptor Alteration.
● Physical inactivity alters the interaction between insulin and its receptors.
● Promotes weight gain, further decreasing insulin sensitivity.
● Leads to impaired glucose tolerance (IGT).

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Contrast the effectiveness of BMI versus Waist-to-Hip ratio in predicting subsequent Type 2 Diabetes risk.
back:
● Waist-to-Hip ratio is a more powerful determinant.
● Reflects visceral/abdominal adiposity rather than total mass.
● Central obesity is specifically linked to insulin resistance.
● BMI measures generalized obesity only.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Identify three specific viral agents and two chemical toxins implicated in the destruction of pancreatic beta cells.
back:
● Viruses: Mumps, Rubella, and Coxsackie B4.
● Toxins: Alloxan and Streptozotocin.
● Mechanism: May trigger autoimmune destruction in genetically susceptible hosts.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus shows a strong association with specific genetic markers, where the highest risk is found in individuals possessing both [___] and [___] alleles.
back:
• HLA-DR3
• HLA-DR4

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old obese male presents with hypertension, dyslipidemia, and fasting hyperglycemia. Explain the pathophysiological link between his central adiposity and high blood pressure.
back:
• Central obesity induces insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinaemia.
• Excessive insulin levels increase sodium retention by renal tubules.
• High insulin also stimulates endothelial proliferation, initiating atherosclerosis and subsequent hypertension.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: How does physical inactivity independently contribute to the development of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus in genetically susceptible individuals?
back:
• Lack of exercise alters the interaction between insulin and its cellular receptors.
• This decreases insulin sensitivity and impairs glucose uptake in skeletal muscles.
• It promotes weight gain, further exacerbating insulin resistance.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
coreConcept: Differential Features of Type 1 vs Type 2 DM
front: Contrast the typical clinical presentation and Ketosis risk of an untreated 12-year-old with autoimmune beta-cell failure versus a 50-year-old obese patient with insulin resistance.
back:
• Type 1 (Child): Abrupt onset, catabolic state, and high risk of ketosis due to absent insulin.
• Type 2 (Adult): Gradual onset, often incidental discovery, and low/slow risk of ketosis.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Identify the dietary fat modifications recommended to improve insulin sensitivity and reduce the risk of progression from Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT) to Type 2 DM.
back:
• Replace saturated fats with unsaturated vegetable fats or polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA).
• Ensure a high intake of dietary fiber (minimum 20g/day).
• Avoid high total fat intake (greater than 37% of energy).

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Maternal diabetes leads to offspring who are heavy at birth; however, those born with intrauterine growth retardation followed by [___] are also at high risk for early-onset Type 2 Diabetes.
back:

• These children have a three-fold higher risk of developing diabetes than those born before the mother developed the disease.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Type 1 diabetes mellitus is strongly associated with the genetic markers HLA-DR3 and [___].

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes
front: Describe the physiological mechanism by which central adiposity leads to the development of Type 2 Diabetes.

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes

category: Describe epidemiological risk factors for Diabetes

front: During a community camp, a 50-year-old sedentary worker has a fasting plasma glucose of 130 mg/dl. Specify the next clinical step to confirm the diagnosis.
back:
Repeat testing on a second occasion:
- A single abnormal value requires confirmation.
- Use 75g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) for definitive diagnosis.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Outline the "Population Strategy" for the primary prevention of Type 2 Diabetes in a developing community.
back:
Primordial and Primary prevention:
- Maintenance of normal body weight.
- Adoption of physical exercise.
- High dietary fiber and avoidance of sweet foods.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Distinguish between Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) and Diabetes Mellitus based on fasting plasma glucose levels.
back:
IFG: Fasting glucose 110–125 mg/dl.
- Diabetes: Fasting glucose ≥ 126 mg/dl.
- Both require venous plasma measurement for accuracy.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: List three host factors that categorize an individual into the "high-risk" group for diabetes screening.
back:
1. Age ≥ 40 years.
- 2. Obesity (central/abdominal adiposity).
- 3. Family history of diabetes in first-degree relatives.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: In community screening for diabetes, urine testing for glucose is often avoided because it lacks [___], leading to a high rate of false-negative results.
back: Sensitivity (10-50%). Many mild or early cases do not exceed the renal threshold for glucose, meaning they are missed if only urine is tested.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old male undergoes screening at a village health camp. His fasting plasma glucose is 118 mg/dl and his 2-hour post-75g glucose load is 130 mg/dl. Identify his glycemic status.
back: Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG). Fasting plasma glucose is between 110-125 mg/dl and the 2-hour value is <140 mg/dl.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Explain the role of the 'Standard Oral Glucose Tolerance Test' (OGTT) as the cornerstone for epidemiological surveys of diabetes.
back: It provides a definitive diagnosis by measuring a 2-hour value after a 75g glucose load. It captures cases that fasting blood sugar tests alone might miss.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Contrast the target of 'Population Strategy' versus 'High-Risk Strategy' in the primary prevention of Type 2 Diabetes.
back: Population Strategy: Targets the whole community to shift lifestyle habits (diet/exercise). High-Risk Strategy: Targets specific individuals (obese, family history, age 40+) for intensive intervention.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Identify the primary clinical utility of measuring Glycosylated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) at six-month intervals for a known diabetic.
back: It provides a long-term index of glycemic control, reflecting the mean blood glucose levels over the preceding 2-3 months (the red cell lifespan).

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: According to WHO recommendations, the threshold for diagnosing diabetes using fasting plasma glucose is [___] mg/dl or higher.
back: 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l). Values below this but above 110 mg/dl fall into the Impaired Fasting Glucose category.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: A 38-year-old obese woman with a family history of diabetes shows a 2-hour plasma glucose of 160 mg/dl and a fasting glucose of 115 mg/dl. Classify this finding.
back: Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT). Defined as fasting <126 mg/dl and 2-hour plasma glucose between 140-200 mg/dl.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: How does the 'Iceberg Phenomenon' apply specifically to the prevalence of Type 2 Diabetes in a community setting?
back: The visible tip represents diagnosed cases. The large submerged portion represents the vast number of undiagnosed, asymptomatic cases that require active screening.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Distinguish between the 2-hour glucose thresholds for 'Impaired Glucose Tolerance' and 'Diabetes Mellitus' following a 75g oral load.
back: IGT: 140 to 199 mg/dl (7.8 to 11.0 mmol/l). Diabetes: 200 mg/dl (11.1 mmol/l) or higher.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Identify three high-risk indicators in women that necessitate targeted screening for diabetes according to community health protocols.
back: 1. History of gestational diabetes. 2. Delivering a baby weighing >4.5 kg. 3. Excess weight gain during pregnancy.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: The preferred gold standard test for definitive epidemiological surveys and community-based case-finding of diabetes is the [___].
back:
Standard Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT).
- Uses a 75g oral glucose load.
- 2-hour plasma glucose value is measured.
- More reliable than fasting glucose alone.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old male presents for a checkup. His fasting plasma glucose is 118 mg/dl and his 2-hour plasma glucose after a 75g load is 135 mg/dl. Identify the diagnosis.
back:
Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG).
- Fasting glucose: 110-125 mg/dl.
- 2-hour glucose: < 140 mg/dl.
- Represents an intermediate 'at-risk' state.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Explain the role of Glycosylated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) in the secondary prevention and monitoring of diabetic patients.
back:
Long-term glycemic index.
- Reflects mean blood glucose over the previous 2-3 months.
- Based on glucose complexing with hemoglobin proportional to concentration.
- Recommended at half-yearly intervals.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Contrast the diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of urine glucose testing for mass community screening.
back:
Sensitivity: Very low (10-50%); misses many mild cases (false-negatives).
- Specificity: High (>90%); few false-positives.
- Conclusion: Inappropriate for mass screening or epidemiological surveys.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Identify the specific obstetric history that classifies a woman as 'high-risk' for diabetes screening in a community setting.
back:
History of delivering large babies.
- Specifically babies weighing >4.5 kg.
- Or >3.5 kg in constitutionally small populations.
- Also includes excessive weight gain during pregnancy.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: According to WHO recommendations, a 2-hour plasma glucose value of [___] mg/dl or higher is diagnostic for Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
200 mg/dl (11.1 mmol/l).
- Measured after 75g oral glucose ingestion.
- Fasting plasma glucose threshold is 126 mg/dl.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: A 50-year-old sedentary obese female has a fasting plasma glucose of 120 mg/dl and a 2-hour post-glucose value of 180 mg/dl. Categorize her glycemic status.
back:
Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT).
- Fasting glucose: < 126 mg/dl.
- 2-hour glucose: 140 mg/dl to 200 mg/dl.
- Defined as an intermediate stage between normal and diabetes.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: How does the 'Iceberg Phenomenon' describe the challenge of Diabetes detection in developing countries?
back:
Iceberg Disease:
- Tip: Known/diagnosed cases.
- Submerged portion: Massive pool of undiagnosed asymptomatic individuals.
- Implication: Mass screening of whole population is unrewarding; target high-risk groups instead.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Distinguish between the target focus of 'Population Strategy' versus 'High-Risk Strategy' in the primary prevention of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
Population Strategy: Targets environmental risk factors globally (healthy nutrition, exercise).
- High-Risk Strategy: Targets specific individuals (obese, family history) to correct sedentary lifestyle and over-nutrition.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: List three physiological factors besides obesity that constitute the 'Insulin Resistance Syndrome' (Syndrome X).
back:
Key components:
- Hyperglycemia.
- Hyperinsulinemia.
- Dyslipidemia.
- Hypertension.
- Leads to accelerated atherosclerosis and stroke.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: In community screening, the standard Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) involves measuring plasma glucose 2 hours after an oral load of [___] grams of glucose.
back: 75 grams. This is the cornerstone for the epidemiological diagnosis of diabetes and impaired glucose tolerance (IGT).

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old obese male presents for a checkup. Lab results show a fasting plasma glucose of 118 mg/dl and a 2-hour post-load glucose of 130 mg/dl. Identify the diagnosis.
back: Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG). Criteria: Fasting glucose 110–125 mg/dl AND 2-hour glucose < 140 mg/dl.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Explain the role of Glycosylated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in secondary prevention and monitoring of diabetes.
back: HbA1c provides a long-term index of glucose control over the previous 2–3 months. It reflects mean blood glucose levels during the red cell lifespan.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
coreConcept: Differential diagnosis of IGT vs Diabetes
front: A community survey reveals several individuals with fasting glucose < 126 mg/dl but 2-hour post-load glucose between 140-199 mg/dl. Contrast this status with a definitive diabetes diagnosis.
back: * Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT): 2-hour glucose 140–199 mg/dl. * Diabetes Mellitus: 2-hour glucose ≥ 200 mg/dl or Fasting ≥ 126 mg/dl.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Identify three high-risk obstetric history factors that necessitate targeted diabetes screening in women.
back: * History of delivering a baby weighing > 4.5 kg. * Excessive weight gain during pregnancy. * Previous diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM).

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: According to WHO criteria, the definitive threshold for diagnosing diabetes with a fasting plasma glucose sample is [___] mg/dl.
back: ≥ 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l). Values between 110–125 mg/dl are classified as Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG).

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: A primary health worker is organizing a 'High-Risk Strategy' for diabetes. List the three most critical host factors (excluding pregnancy) for group selection.
