back: * Age 40 years and over. * Obesity (specifically central/abdominal adiposity). * Positive family history of diabetes.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Explain why urine glucose testing, despite being inexpensive, is not recommended for epidemiological surveys of diabetes.
back: Low Sensitivity (10–50%). It yields too many false-negatives, missing milder cases of the disease where glycosuria is absent.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Contrast the 'Population Strategy' of diabetes prevention with the 'High-Risk Strategy' regarding their primary objectives.
back: * Population Strategy: Aims at lifestyle/dietary changes for the whole community to shift the entire risk curve. * High-Risk Strategy: Targets individuals with obesity or family history for specific interventions.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Identify the screening finding that classifies a patient as having 'Impaired Glucose Tolerance' (IGT) during a 75g OGTT.
back: A 2-hour plasma glucose level between 140 mg/dl and 200 mg/dl (7.8 to 11.1 mmol/l).

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Primordial prevention of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus primarily focuses on preventing the emergence of risk factors by maintaining [___] and adopting healthy nutritional habits.
back:
• Normal body weight
• Regular physical exercise
• High intake of dietary fiber
• Avoidance of sweet foods

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old sedentary male presents with a fasting plasma glucose of 118 mg/dl. According to WHO recommendations, this finding represents [___].
back:
• Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG)
• Glucose range: 110 to 125 mg/dl
• Requires intervention to prevent progression to overt Diabetes

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Describe the mechanism by which glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) provides a long-term index of glycemic control in secondary prevention.
back:
• Glucose complexes with hemoglobin proportional to blood concentration
• Reflects mean glucose over red cell lifespan
• Indicates control over previous 2–3 months

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Contrast the blood glucose thresholds used to distinguish Diabetes Mellitus from Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT) in a 2-hour post-75g glucose load test.
back:
• Diabetes: ≥ 200 mg/dl (11.1 mmol/l)
• IGT: 140 to < 200 mg/dl (7.8 to 11.1 mmol/l)
• IGT is an 'at-risk' intermediate state

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Outline the three fundamental pillars of treatment for a newly diagnosed diabetic patient to prevent complications.
back:
• Diet alone (small balanced meals)
• Diet combined with oral antidiabetic drugs
• Diet combined with insulin
• Aim: Maintain blood glucose within normal limits

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Screening for diabetes is most effective in high-risk groups, including women who have delivered a baby weighing more than [___] kg.
back:
• 4.5 kg (Macrosomia)
• Other high-risk groups: Obese, age >40, family history, and patients with premature atherosclerosis

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: A diabetic patient is educated on daily foot inspections and the use of Doppler ultrasound to check circulation. This intervention is a component of [___] prevention.
back:
• Tertiary prevention
• Aim: To prevent disability (gangrene/amputation)
• Focuses on managing established complications

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Explain the difference between the 'Population Strategy' and 'High-risk Strategy' in the primary prevention of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Population: Community-wide lifestyle/dietary changes and NCD program integration
• High-risk: Targeted weight loss and exercise for obese/prediabetic individuals

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Distinguish between the primary prevention goals for Type 1 vs. Type 2 Diabetes based on current epidemiological knowledge.
back:
• Type 1: Limited scope; no current practical justification for prevention/genetic counseling
• Type 2: High scope; focuses on eliminating environmental risk factors (obesity/sedentary life)

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: List the key elements of 'Self-care' that patients must adopt in secondary prevention to optimize primary health care outcomes.
back:
• Adherence to diet and drugs
• Self-monitoring of blood glucose/urine
• Recognition of hypoglycemic symptoms
• Regular foot care and weight maintenance

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: For community screening, the common practice of testing urine for glucose is ideally performed [___] after a meal.
back: Two hours. (Note: This method lacks sensitivity for mild cases, leading to frequent false negatives).

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old male with a family history of diabetes undergoes an OGTT. His fasting plasma glucose is 115 mg/dl and his 2-hour post-glucose value is 190 mg/dl. Determine his glucose status.
back:
Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT).
- Fasting < 126 mg/dl.
- 2-hour glucose between 140-200 mg/dl.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Explain the biological rationale for using glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) as a tool for secondary prevention in diabetes.
back:
- Glucose complexes with hemoglobin proportional to blood concentration.
- Reflects mean glycemic levels over the preceding 2-3 months (red cell lifespan).

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: A sedentary 50-year-old patient with central obesity and hypertension presents for a checkup. Contrast the utility of urine testing versus blood sugar testing for his initial screening.
back:
- Urine: High specificity (>90%) but low sensitivity (10-50%); misses mild cases.
- Blood: OGTT (2-hour 75g) is the diagnostic cornerstone for accuracy.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Identify the high-risk criteria involving obstetric history that mandate screening a woman for Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
- History of delivering a baby weighing >4.5 kg (or 3.5 kg in smaller populations).
- Excessive weight gain during pregnancy.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: According to WHO recommendations, the threshold for diagnosing Diabetes Mellitus using fasting plasma glucose is [___] mg/dl.
back: >= 126 mg/dl (or 7.0 mmol/l).

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: A community program aims to implement a 'population strategy' for the primary prevention of Type 2 Diabetes. Which lifestyle modifications should be prioritized?
back:
- Maintaining normal body weight.
- High dietary fiber intake (e.g., 20g minimum).
- Regular physical exercise to improve insulin sensitivity.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Describe the physiological objective of performing periodic foot examinations in diabetic patients at the primary care level.
back:
- Detect defective blood circulation via Doppler probes.
- Identify loss of sensation (neuropathy).
- Screen for skin health to prevent non-traumatic amputations.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Distinguish between the clinical significance of Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) and Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT).
back:
- IFG: Fasting 110-125 mg/dl; 2-h glucose < 140 mg/dl.
- IGT: Fasting < 126 mg/dl; 2-h glucose 140-200 mg/dl.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: State the screening age threshold and primary physical risk factor used to identify 'high-risk' groups for targeted community screening.
back:
- Age: 40 years and over.
- Physical Factor: Obesity (particularly central/abdominal adiposity).

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: The biochemical process where glucose complexes with a specific fraction of hemoglobin to provide a 2–3 month glycemic history is known as [___].
back:
• Glycosylation (resulting in HbA1c).
• Proportional to blood glucose concentration.
• Provides a long-term index of control.
• Useful in secondary prevention.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: A 42-year-old female with a history of delivering a 4.8 kg infant presents for a check-up. Her random blood sugar is 160 mg/dl. State the next most appropriate screening step.
back:
• Perform a Standard Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT).
• History of macrosomia (>4.5 kg) defines a high-risk group.
• Random samples are insufficient for epidemiological diagnosis.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Explain how the 'Iceberg phenomenon' applies to the prevalence of Diabetes Mellitus in a community setting.
back:
• Visible Tip: Diagnosed, symptomatic clinical cases.
• Submerged Mass: Undiagnosed, asymptomatic, or 'at-risk' (IGT/IFG) individuals.
• Screening: Essential to identify the massive undetected burden.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Contrast the diagnostic thresholds for Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) in 'Impaired Fasting Glucose' (IFG) versus 'Diabetes Mellitus' according to WHO guidelines.
back:
• IFG: 110 mg/dl to 125 mg/dl (6.1–6.9 mmol/l).
• Diabetes Mellitus: ≥ 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l).
• IFG represents an intermediate 'at-risk' state.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Identify the limitations of using urine examination for glucose 2 hours after a meal in mass community screening.
back:
• Poor Sensitivity: Misses 50–90% of cases (high false-negatives).
• Poor for surveys: Many mild diabetics lack glycosuria.
• Specificity: High (>90%), but inadequate for case-finding.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: In mass screening for diabetes, the WHO diagnostic threshold for a 2-hour plasma glucose value after a 75g oral glucose load is [___] mg/dl or higher.
back:
• 200 mg/dl (11.1 mmol/l).
• Cornerstone of epidemiological diagnosis.
• Values between 140–200 mg/dl indicate Impaired Glucose Tolerance.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: The stage of prevention focusing on preventing the emergence of risk factors like obesity and sedentary lifestyle in populations where they have not yet appeared is [___] prevention.
back:
Primordial Prevention.
- Targets healthy lifestyle adoption in children and adolescents.
- Focuses on nutritional habits and physical activity.
- Aims to stop risk factor development early.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old obese male with a family history of diabetes is screened using a 75g oral glucose load. A 2-hour plasma glucose value of 160 mg/dl indicates [___].
back:
Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT).
- Intermediate 'at-risk' state (140-200 mg/dl).
- Significant risk factor for future Type 2 Diabetes.
- Requires aggressive lifestyle secondary prevention.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Explain the components of the 'Population Strategy' for primary prevention of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
- Maintenance of normal body weight.
- Adoption of healthy nutritional habits (high fiber, low sugar).
- Regular physical exercise.
- Integration into community-based NCD control programs.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Contrast the scope of primary prevention for Type 1 Diabetes versus Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
- Type 1: Limited scope; no current practical justification for genetic counseling or prevention.
- Type 2: Broad scope; targets environmental risk factors like obesity, diet, and physical inactivity.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
coreConcept: Role of HbA1c in Diabetes Management
front: Identify the clinical utility of measuring glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) at half-yearly intervals in a known diabetic patient.
back:
- Long-term index of glucose control.
- Reflects mean blood glucose over the previous 2-3 months.
- Essential for monitoring secondary prevention efficacy.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: According to WHO recommendations, the threshold fasting plasma glucose level for the definitive diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus is [___] mg/dl.
back:
≥ 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l).
- Alternative: 2-hour plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dl.
- Cornerstone of secondary prevention (early diagnosis).

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: A patient with chronic diabetic foot ulcers is referred to a specialized clinic for Doppler ultrasound and intensive wound care. This is an example of [___] prevention.
back:
Tertiary Prevention.
- Focuses on disability limitation and rehabilitation.
- Aims to prevent gangrene, blindness, and renal failure.
- Utilizes specialized diabetic clinics.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Describe the 'High-Risk Strategy' for primary prevention in individuals predisposed to Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
- Targeted weight reduction in obese subjects.
- Avoiding diabetogenic drugs (e.g., oral contraceptives).
- Controlling atherosclerosis factors (smoking, blood pressure, cholesterol).
- Alcohol abstinence.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Distinguish between Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT) and Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) based on plasma glucose levels.
back:
- IGT: 2-hour post-glucose 140–200 mg/dl (Fasting < 126).
- IFG: Fasting plasma glucose 110–125 mg/dl (2-hour < 140).

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: List four crucial elements of 'Self-care' education in the secondary prevention of diabetes.
back:
- Adherence to diet and drug regimens.
- Self-monitoring of blood glucose.
- Regular foot self-examination.
- Recognition of hypoglycemic symptoms.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Diabetes is often referred to as an "[___]" disease because the number of undiagnosed cases in the community far exceeds the known cases.
back:
Iceberg
- Most cases in the community are undiagnosed or subclinical.
- The "tip" represents diagnosed cases.
- The submerged portion represents undiagnosed/at-risk individuals.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old obese male undergoes screening. His fasting plasma glucose is 118 mg/dl. According to WHO criteria, this finding is classified as [___].
back:
Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG)
- Fasting plasma glucose: 110–125 mg/dl (6.1–6.9 mmol/l).
- 2-hour post-glucose load (if measured) must be < 140 mg/dl.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
coreConcept: Limitations of Urine Screening for Diabetes
front: Explain why urine glucose testing, performed 2 hours after a meal, is considered an inappropriate tool for large-scale community screening.
back:
Poor Sensitivity (10-50%)
- Yields many false-negatives (misses mild cases).
- Renal threshold varies.
- Not specific enough compared to blood sugar testing.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Contrast the diagnostic 2-hour post-75g glucose load values required for "Impaired Glucose Tolerance" (IGT) versus "Diabetes Mellitus."
back:
IGT vs. Diabetes:
- IGT: 140 to < 200 mg/dl (7.8–11.1 mmol/l).
- Diabetes: ≥ 200 mg/dl (≥ 11.1 mmol/l).
- Fasting must be < 126 mg/dl for IGT.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Identify three specific obstetric or history-based "High-Risk" groups that should be prioritized for targeted diabetes screening.
back:
High-Risk Target Groups:
- Women with history of baby > 4.5 kg.
- Women with excessive weight gain during pregnancy.
- Individuals with family history of diabetes or premature atherosclerosis.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: The gold standard test for the long-term index of glycemic control, reflecting the mean blood glucose over the previous 2–3 months, is [___].
back:
Glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
- Reflects red cell life-time (8-12 weeks).
- Proportional to mean blood glucose levels.
- Measured at half-yearly intervals for monitoring.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: A 52-year-old female with a BMI of 32 presents with a random plasma glucose of 185 mg/dl. What is the definitive epidemiological tool recommended by WHO for diagnosis?
back:
Standard Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT)
- Uses 75g oral glucose load.
- 2-hour plasma value is the cornerstone of diagnosis.
- Random glucose is considered unsatisfactory for definitive diagnosis.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Describe the "Population Strategy" for the primary prevention of Type 2 Diabetes in a community.
back:
Primordial/Primary Prevention:
- Shifting the whole community's risk via lifestyle changes.
- Maintaining normal body weight.
- Promoting high dietary fiber and physical exercise.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: Distinguish between "Android" and "Gynoid" obesity in the context of metabolic risk for Diabetes.
back:
Android vs. Gynoid:
- Android: Abdominal/visceral fat; high risk for insulin resistance (Syndrome X).
- Gynoid: Peripheral distribution; lower metabolic risk.
- Waist-to-hip ratio is a powerful determinant of risk.

category: Screening of community for Diabetes
front: State the WHO diagnostic threshold for Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) to confirm Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
≥ 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l)
- Patient must be in a true fasting state.
- Values below 110 mg/dl are considered normal fasting levels.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Prevention of the emergence of risk factors for diabetes (e.g., healthy lifestyle education for children) in countries where they have not yet appeared is termed [___] prevention.
back:
Primordial Prevention.
- Targets social and environmental patterns.
- Focuses on discouraging the adoption of harmful lifestyles (sedentary habits, poor diet).

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old obese male with a family history of diabetes is asymptomatic. According to WHO criteria, a fasting plasma glucose of [___] mg/dl or higher is diagnostic for Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l).
- Alternatively, a 2-hour plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dl.
- This falls under case-finding in secondary prevention.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Explain the rationale for measuring glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA1c) as a long-term index of glucose control in secondary prevention.
back:
- Glucose complexes with haemoglobin proportional to blood concentration.
- Reflects mean blood glucose levels over the red cell life-time (previous 2–3 months).
- Recommended at half-yearly intervals.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Contrast the primary objective of the 'Population Strategy' with the 'High-risk Strategy' in the primary prevention of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
- Population Strategy: Broad elimination of environmental risk factors (diet/exercise) for the whole community.
- High-risk Strategy: Targets specific individuals (obese, family history) for intensive lifestyle modification.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Identify the specific metabolic markers characterizing the 'Insulin Resistance Syndrome' (Syndrome X) that increase cardiovascular risk in obese diabetics.
back:
- Hyperglycaemia and Hyperinsulinaemia.
- Dyslipidaemia (high triglycerides).
- Hypertension (via renal sodium retention).
- Endothelial proliferation initiating atherosclerosis.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: The intermediate 'at-risk' state between diabetes and normality, defined by a 2-hour post-glucose load between 140 and 200 mg/dl, is [___].
back:
Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT).
- Fasting glucose must be < 126 mg/dl.
- Represents a critical target group for primary prevention (lifestyle/metformin).

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: A diabetic patient presents with loss of sensation in the feet. Under which level of prevention does routine Doppler ultrasound examination for circulation fall?
back:
Secondary Prevention.
- Aims to prevent complications (diabetic foot/gangrene).
- Includes early detection of vascular and neurological impairment.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Outline the role of 'Self-care' as a component of secondary prevention in diabetic management.
back:
- Patient takes major responsibility for care.
- Includes: Adherence to drug/diet, blood glucose monitoring, foot exams, and recognizing hypoglycaemia symptoms.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Distinguish between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes based on their primary prevention potential according to current medical evidence.
back:
- Type 1: Scope is limited; no practical population or high-risk strategy available.
- Type 2: High potential via correcting obesity, physical inactivity, and dietary fat quality.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: State the minimum recommended daily intake of dietary fibre (NSP) for the nutritional control and prevention of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
20 grams.
- High intake reduces blood glucose and insulin levels.
- Found in whole grains, vegetables, and fruits.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Primordial prevention of Diabetes mellitus primarily focuses on the [___] of risk factors such as obesity and sedentary lifestyles in populations where they haven't yet appeared.
back: - Prevention of the emergence of risk factors. - Focuses on maintaining healthy nutritional habits. - Encourages physical exercise from an early age.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old obese male with a family history of diabetes undergoes screening. His 2-hour plasma glucose after a 75g oral load is 180 mg/dl. This finding indicates [___].
back: - Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT). - Represents an 'at-risk' intermediate state. - Defined by 2-h values between 140-200 mg/dl.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Explain how physical activity serves as a primary prevention tool for Type 2 Diabetes at the cellular level.
back: - Improves insulin sensitivity. - Enhances interaction between insulin and its receptors. - Increases glucose uptake by skeletal muscle.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Contrast the Population Strategy with the High-Risk Strategy in the primary prevention of Type 2 Diabetes.
back: - Population Strategy: Whole-community lifestyle changes (dietary fiber/weight). - High-Risk Strategy: Targeted interventions for obese or family-history positive individuals. - Population strategy shifts the entire curve.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Identify the clinical significance of monitoring Glycosylated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) every six months in a known diabetic patient.
back: - Provides a long-term index (2-3 months) of control. - Proportional to mean blood glucose levels. - Essential for secondary prevention to detect suboptimal treatment.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: According to WHO diagnostic criteria, Diabetes Mellitus is confirmed if the fasting plasma glucose is equal to or greater than [___] mg/dl.
back: - 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l). - Alternatively, 2-h plasma glucose >= 200 mg/dl. - Venous plasma is the gold standard.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: An asymptomatic 50-year-old woman is found to have glycosuria during a routine check-up. State the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis.
back: - Standard Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT). - Urine testing is insensitive and yields false negatives. - Blood glucose is the cornerstone of diagnosis.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Direct how tertiary prevention measures aim to reduce the Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) in diabetic populations.
back: - Specialized Diabetic Clinics for advanced care. - Management of complications (blindness, gangrene, renal failure). - Intensive clinical and epidemiological research.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Distinguish between the diagnostic fasting plasma glucose ranges for Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) and Diabetes Mellitus.
back: - IFG: 110 to 125 mg/dl (6.1-6.9 mmol/l). - Diabetes: >= 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l). - Both represent hyperglycemic states with varying risk.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Mention the specific high-risk groups for whom diabetes screening is most rewarding in a resource-limited setting like Pakistan.
back: - Age 40+ years. - Obese individuals. - Women with history of babies >4.5 kg. - Those with family history of diabetes.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: The prevention of the emergence of risk factors for diabetes, such as urbanization and unhealthy dietary habits, in populations where they have not yet appeared is termed [___] prevention.
back:
Primordial Prevention.

*   Focuses on preventing environmental/lifestyle risk factors.
*   Maintenance of normal body weight from childhood.
*   Promotion of healthy nutritional habits in society.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old obese male with a strong family history of Type 2 DM is advised to undergo regular physical activity and a high-fiber diet to avoid developing hyperglycemia. This intervention belongs to [___].
back:
Primary Prevention (High-risk strategy).

*   Targets individuals with specific risk factors.
*   Aims to prevent the onset of clinical disease.
*   Correction of sedentary lifestyle and over-nutrition.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Explain the role of Glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) in the secondary prevention and monitoring of Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
HbA1c Monitoring:

*   Provides a long-term index of glucose control (previous 2-3 months).
*   Glucose complexes with hemoglobin proportional to blood concentration.
*   Assessed at half-yearly intervals to prevent/detect complications.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Contrast the 'Population Strategy' with the 'High-Risk Strategy' used in the primary prevention of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
Comparison:

*   Population Strategy: Targets the entire community; promotes community-wide healthy nutrition and activity.
*   High-Risk Strategy: Targets specific susceptible groups (obese, family history); requires personalized medical guidance and motivation.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Discuss why urine glucose testing is considered an inappropriate tool for mass screening in the secondary prevention of diabetes.
back:
Inadequacies of Urine Testing:

*   Low sensitivity (10-50%); misses many mild/asymptomatic cases.
*   Produces many false-negatives.
*   Glycosuria may occur in non-diabetics (false-positives).

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: According to WHO diagnostic criteria, Diabetes Mellitus is confirmed if the 2-hour plasma glucose after a 75g oral load is greater than or equal to [___] mg/dl.
back:
200 mg/dl (11.1 mmol/l).

*   Gold standard: Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT).
*   Fasting plasma glucose threshold: ≥ 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l).

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: A diabetic patient presents for an annual eye exam and daily foot inspection for sensation loss. These specific actions represent which sub-level of prevention?
back:
Secondary Prevention.

*   Aims for early diagnosis and treatment.
*   Prevents/delays progression to complications like retinopathy.
*   Includes patient 'Self-care' and adherence to drug regimens.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Detail the main objectives of organized 'Diabetic Clinics' at the tertiary level of prevention.
back:
Tertiary Level Objectives:

*   Organize specialized management to limit disability (e.g., laser for blindness).
*   Organize rehabilitation for complications like gangrene or renal failure.
*   Conduct clinical and epidemiological research.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Contrast the scope of primary prevention between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
Type 1 vs Type 2 Scope:

*   Type 1: Limited/not appropriate as current knowledge cannot prevent autoimmune beta-cell destruction.
*   Type 2: Possible and effective through elimination of environmental risk factors like obesity.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Identify the six 'High-Risk' groups that should be targeted for diabetes screening in the community.
back:
Target Groups for Screening:

*   Age 40 and over.
*   Obese individuals.
*   Family history of diabetes.
*   Women with previous baby weight >4.5kg.
*   Excess weight gain during pregnancy.
*   Patients with premature atherosclerosis.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Prevention aimed at avoiding the emergence of risk factors for Type 2 Diabetes in populations where they have not yet appeared is known as [___] prevention.
back:
• Primordial prevention
• Focuses on maintaining healthy lifestyles and nutritional habits
• Targets the avoidance of urbanization-related sedentary behaviors

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old obese male shows a fasting plasma glucose (FPG) of 130 mg/dl on two separate occasions. State the diagnosis based on WHO threshold criteria.
back:
• Diagnosis: Diabetes Mellitus
• WHO FPG Threshold: ≥ 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l)
• Requires two abnormal tests or clinical symptoms for confirmation

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Explain the biochemical rationale for utilizing Glycosylated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) as a long-term index of glycemic control in secondary prevention.
back:
• Glucose complexes with hemoglobin proportional to blood concentration
• Reflects mean glucose levels over the red cell lifespan
• Provides an index for the previous 2–3 months

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Contrast the 'Population Strategy' with the 'High-Risk Strategy' regarding the primary prevention of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Population Strategy: Massive shifts in socio-environmental factors (e.g., diet, exercise) for the whole community
• High-Risk Strategy: Intensive lifestyle interventions for susceptible individuals (e.g., obese, family history)

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: List four essential periodic clinical assessments required for a diabetic patient to facilitate effective secondary prevention of complications.
back:
• Blood Pressure (Target < 130/80 mmHg)
• Foot Examination (circulatory health and sensation)
• Visual Acuity/Retinal screening
• Urine protein and ketone monitoring

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: In an Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT), a 2-hour plasma glucose value ranging from [___] to [___] mg/dl defines Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT).
back:
• 140 mg/dl to 200 mg/dl (7.8 to 11.1 mmol/l)
• Fasting glucose must be < 126 mg/dl
• Represents an 'at-risk' intermediate hyperglycemic state

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: A diabetic patient with established peripheral neuropathy and chronic ulcers is referred to a specialized clinic. Categorize this level of prevention and its primary goal.
back:
• Tertiary Prevention
• Goal: Minimize disability and prevent further complications (e.g., gangrene/amputation)
• Focus: Specialized management and rehabilitation

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: How does the 'Self-Care' component of secondary prevention empower a diabetic patient to manage their metabolic loop effectively?
back:
• Patient adherence to diet and drug regimens
• Regular self-monitoring of blood glucose/urine
• Early recognition of hypoglycemia or glycosuria symptoms
• Maintaining optimum weight and foot hygiene

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Contrast the diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of urine glucose testing with blood glucose testing in mass screening programs.
back:
• Urine Test: High specificity (>90%) but low sensitivity (10-50%); misses mild/early cases
• Blood Test: Cornerstone of diagnosis; 2-hour post-glucose is most reliable for surveys

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Identify three obstetric history factors that place a woman in the 'High-Risk' category for Diabetes screening.
back:
• Previous baby weighing > 4.5 kg
• History of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
• Excess weight gain during pregnancy

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Prevention aimed at avoiding the emergence of risk factors like obesity and sedentary lifestyles in societies where they have not yet appeared is termed [___] prevention.
back:
Primordial Prevention.
- Focuses on maintaining normal body weight.
- Encourages healthy nutritional habits and exercise early in life.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: A 45-year-old obese male with a family history of diabetes undergoes a 2-hour 75g oral glucose tolerance test. His result is 160 mg/dl. Identify his clinical category and the level of prevention applied.
back:
Category: Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT).
- Prevention: Secondary Prevention.
- Aim: Early detection to prevent progression to overt diabetes.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Explain the role of Glycosylated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) monitoring as a tool in the secondary prevention of diabetes.
back:
Index of long-term glucose control.
- Reflects mean blood glucose over the previous 2–3 months.
- Performed half-yearly to adjust treatment and prevent complications.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Contrast the 'Population Strategy' and 'High-risk Strategy' as applied to the primary prevention of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
Population: Lifestyle changes for the whole community (diet/exercise).
- High-risk: Targets specific individuals (obese/sedentary) for weight loss and avoidance of diabetogenic drugs.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Outline the primary objectives of tertiary prevention in a patient already suffering from long-standing Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
Establish specialized diabetic clinics.
- Manage complications (blindness, renal failure, gangrene).
- Provide rehabilitation to limit disability and improve quality of life.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: According to WHO recommendations, a fasting plasma glucose level of [___] mg/dl or higher is the diagnostic threshold for Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/l).
- Venous plasma glucose is the standard sample.
- Used for early case finding in high-risk groups.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: A diabetic patient is taught to perform daily foot examinations and recognize symptoms of hypoglycemia. This specific intervention falls under [___] prevention.
back:
Secondary Prevention (Self-care).
- Adherence to diet/drug regimens.
- Responsibility for blood glucose monitoring and early symptom recognition.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Describe why diabetes is referred to as an 'iceberg disease' and its implication for secondary prevention.
back:
Undiagnosed cases represent the submerged part.
- Symptomatic cases are only the visible 'tip'.
- Implication: Targeted screening is essential to find hidden cases.

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: Distinguish the scope of primary prevention between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus based on current community medicine guidelines.
back:
Type 1: Limited scope; primary prevention is currently not appropriate.
- Type 2: Effective through environmental risk factor elimination (obesity, inactivity, dietary fats).

category: Apply levels of prevention for control of Diabetes
front: List four high-risk groups prioritized for diabetes screening in the primary healthcare setting.
back:
Obese individuals.
- Age 40 years and older.
- Positive family history of diabetes.
- Women with history of babies weighing >4.5 kg.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Genetic disorders are broadly classified into three categories: Chromosomal abnormalities, Unifactorial (Mendelian) diseases, and [___] disorders.
back: Multifactorial disorders (involving multiple genes and environmental factors).

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A child born to a mother of advanced age presents with short stature, tilted eye-slits, and mental retardation. The underlying chromosomal mechanism is usually [___].
back: Trisomy 21 (Down's Syndrome), typically resulting from meiotic non-disjunction.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Explain how consanguineous marriages (first-cousin unions) impact the prevalence of genetic diseases in the community.
back: They increase the probability of both parents carrying the same recessive mutant gene, leading to a higher frequency of autosomal recessive disorders in offspring.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Contrast the inheritance risk for daughters and sons if a hemophilia-affected male marries a normal female.
back: All daughters will be carriers (100%), while all sons will be normal (0%), as the X-linked gene is only passed to daughters.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Identify the primary characteristic of multifactorial disorders regarding their aetiology and community prevalence.
back: They result from the interaction of a polygenic genetic predisposition and environmental triggers (e.g., hypertension, diabetes, or coronary heart disease).

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A female presenting with short stature, primary amenorrhea, and underdeveloped sex glands typically has a [___] sex chromosome constitution.
back: 45,XO (Turner's Syndrome).

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: In a community with a high malaria burden, a point mutation in the beta-globin chain leads to sickling of red blood cells. Name this autosomal recessive disorder.
back: Sickle Cell Anaemia (Homozgyous state HbSS).

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Describe the core function of Genetic Counselling in the context of community preventive medicine.
back: Assessing the risk of hereditary disorders in families and providing information on contraception, prenatal diagnosis, or sterilization to prevent recurrence.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Distinguish between the terms 'Genotype' and 'Phenotype' in genetic medicine.
back: Genotype is the fixed total genetic constitution; Phenotype is the plastic, outward expression influenced by both genes and environment.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: List three high-yield examples of Autosomal Dominant disorders commonly identified in clinical practice.
back: Achondroplasia, Huntington’s Chorea, and Polycystic Kidney Disease.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Genetic disorders resulting from the interplay of multiple genes and environmental factors, such as essential hypertension and diabetes mellitus, are classified as [___] disorders.
back:
* Multifactorial disorders
* Involve complex interactions between heredity and lifestyle
* Account for most common adult chronic diseases (e.g., CHD, schizophrenia).

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A tall 20-year-old male presents with gynecomastia, scanty body hair, and small, non-functional testes. Karyotype analysis for this individual is most likely to reveal [___].
back:
* Klinefelter's Syndrome (47, XXY)
* Sex chromosome aneuploidy in males
* Results in infertility, absent spermatozoa, and mental retardation.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Describe the cellular mechanism of 'non-disjunction' and its significance in the pathogenesis of numerical chromosomal abnormalities.
back:
* Failure of homologous chromosomes or chromatids to separate during division
* Results in aneuploidy (cells with 45 or 47 chromosomes)
* Leading cause of Trisomy 21 (Down's Syndrome).

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Contrast the inheritance risk of an Autosomal Dominant trait with an Autosomal Recessive trait when one parent is an affected heterozygote and the other is normal.
back:
* Autosomal Dominant: 50% risk of affected offspring per pregnancy
* Autosomal Recessive: 0% affected (but 100% carriers) if the other parent is non-carrier
* Dominant traits affect every generation; Recessive traits often skip generations.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Identify the primary category of genetic disorders that follow Mendelian laws and include conditions like Haemophilia and Phenylketonuria.
back:
* Unifactorial (Single-gene) diseases
* Classified into Autosomal Dominant, Autosomal Recessive, and Sex-linked
* Occur due to mutations at a single gene locus.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: The structural chromosomal abnormality where a segment of a chromosome breaks away and attaches to a non-homologous chromosome is termed [___].
back:
* Translocation
* Can be balanced or unbalanced
* A significant mechanism in some inherited cases of Down's Syndrome.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A newborn girl presents with a webbed neck, short stature, and coarctation of the aorta. What is the clinical name and chromosomal constitution of this condition?
back:
* Turner's Syndrome (45, XO)
* Monosomy of the X chromosome
* Leads to primary amenorrhea and underdeveloped sex glands.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Explain the difference between 'Prospective' and 'Retrospective' genetic counseling in a community setting.
back:
* Prospective: Identifying carriers before birth of affected children (e.g., Thalassemia screening)
* Retrospective: Counseling after a disorder has already occurred in the family
* Prospective counseling allows for true disease prevention.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Distinguish between the terms 'Genotype' and 'Phenotype' regarding their stability and expression in an individual.
back:
* Genotype: Total genetic constitution; relatively stable/fixed
* Phenotype: Outward expression of genes; plastic and influenced by environment
* Medicine is often defined as the management of the human phenotype.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Identify three high-yield examples of 'Sex-linked Recessive' disorders commonly tested in community medicine.
back:
* Haemophilia (Type A and B)
* Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
* Colour Blindness
* G6PD Deficiency.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Genetic disorders are broadly classified into three categories: Chromosomal abnormalities, Unifactorial (Mendelian) diseases, and [___] disorders.
back:
Multifactorial disorders.
- Involves multiple genes interacting with environmental factors.
- Common in adult-onset chronic diseases (e.g., Hypertension, Diabetes).

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A 42-year-old pregnant woman is concerned about her baby's risk for intellectual disability and cardiac defects. The most likely chromosomal abnormality associated with advanced maternal age is [___].
back:
Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21).
- Caused by an extra chromosome 21 (Non-disjunction).
- Risk rises from 1:3000 at age 20 to 1:50 at age 45.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Explain the transmission pattern and offspring risk when an affected male with Hemophilia A (X-linked recessive) marries a normal, non-carrier female.
back:
- All daughters become obligate carriers.
- All sons are normal (cannot inherit X-linked trait from father).
- 0% risk of clinically affected children in this specific union.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Contrast Prospective and Retrospective Genetic Counselling as utilized in community medicine.
back:
- Prospective: Screening carriers *before* marriage/birth to prevent first occurrence (e.g., Thalassemia screening).
- Retrospective: Counselling *after* an affected child is already born to the family.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Identify three high-yield clinical examples of Autosomal Dominant (AD) disorders common in the community.
back:
- Achondroplasia (Dwarfism).
- Polydactyly (Extra digits).
- Familial Polyposis Coli.
- Huntington's Chorea.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A phenotypic female presenting with short stature, webbed neck, and primary amenorrhoea likely has a sex chromosome constitution of [___].
back:
45, XO (Turner's Syndrome).
- Results from non-disjunction.
- Features include underdeveloped ovaries and cardiovascular malformations.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A neonate is screened via the Guthrie test and found to have a deficiency in phenylalanine hydroxylase. What is the diagnosis and the primary nutritional intervention?
back:
Phenylketonuria (PKU).
- Intervention: Immediate low-phenylalanine diet.
- Prevents toxic accumulation and subsequent mental retardation.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Describe the central principle of the Hardy-Weinberg Law regarding gene pool stability.
back:
- Allele frequencies remain constant across generations in large, random-mating populations.
- Stability requires absence of mutation, natural selection, and migration.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Distinguish between the goals of Negative Eugenics and Positive Eugenics.
back:
- Negative: Reducing genetic defects by discouraging reproduction in affected individuals.
- Positive: Encouraging breeding among those with desirable, socially valuable traits.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: State the most common procedure used at 14-16 weeks gestation to diagnose chromosomal and metabolic defects in high-risk pregnancies.
back:
Amniocentesis.
- Karyotyping of fetal cells detects aneuploidy.
- Biochemical analysis of fluid detects metabolic errors.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Genetic disorders caused by an extra chromosome resulting in a total count of 47 (instead of 46) are specifically termed [___].
back:
• Trisomies.
• Common example: Down's Syndrome (Trisomy 21).
• Occur due to non-disjunction during cell division.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A newborn boy presents with small testes, gynaecomastia, and scanty body hair. Karyotyping reveals a 47,XXY constitution. Identify the underlying condition.
back:
• Klinefelter’s Syndrome.
• A common sex-chromosome aneuploidy in males.
• Leads to eunuchoid features and infertility.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Explain the stabilizing principle of the Hardy-Weinberg law in population genetics.
back:
• Relative frequencies of each gene allele tend to remain constant across generations.
• Assumes random mating and absence of mutation or migration.
• Used to study the 'gene pool' of a community.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Contrast the preventive objectives of Negative Eugenics with those of Positive Eugenics.
back:
• Negative: Reducing hereditary defects by debarring affected individuals or carriers from procreating (e.g., sterilization).
• Positive: Encouraging individuals with desirable genotypes to assume the burden of parenthood.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Describe the primary developmental mechanism of multifactorial disorders such as Diabetes and Hypertension.
back:
• Complex interaction between polygenic inheritance and environmental triggers.
• Risk factors include obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and diet.
• Higher community prevalence than Mendelian diseases.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: The inheritance pattern characterized by a mutant gene on the X-chromosome that expresses readily in males but is masked in heterozygous females is [___].
back:
• Sex-linked (X-linked) Recessive.
• Examples: Haemophilia, Color blindness, G6PD deficiency.
• Affected males transmit the gene to all daughters (carriers).

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A 40-year-old pregnant female requests screening for fetal chromosomal anomalies. State the most definitive diagnostic procedure and the ideal timing.
back:
• Amniocentesis.
• Performed at 14–16 weeks of pregnancy.
• Involves karyotyping and biochemical analysis of fetal cells.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Summarize the genetic impact of consanguineous marriages on the incidence of community health disorders.
back:
• Increases the risk of bringing together rare recessive genes from a common ancestor.
• Results in offspring homozygous for deleterious recessive traits.
• Higher rates of albinism, PKU, and premature death.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Distinguish between 'Genotype' and 'Phenotype' in the context of human clinical genetics.
back:
• Genotype: The fixed, total genetic constitution (e.g., genetic code for Blood Group A).
• Phenotype: The outward, plastic expression or physical manifestation (e.g., observed height or blood group).

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: List the three major classifications of genetic disorders as prioritized in community medicine.
back:
• Chromosomal abnormalities (Numerical or Structural).
• Unifactorial (Single gene/Mendelian) diseases.
• Multifactorial disorders (Polygenic + Environmental).

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: The numerical abnormality where the total chromosome count is not an exact multiple of the haploid number, seen in conditions like Trisomy 21 or Turner's syndrome, is termed [___].
back:
Aneuploidy.
- Caused by non-disjunction during nuclear division.
- Results in a count of 45 or 47 chromosomes instead of 46.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A 1-year-old child presents with chronic hemolytic anemia, jaundice, and hepatomegaly. Labs confirm a point mutation causing defective globin chain synthesis. Identify the most likely genetic classification of this disorder.
back:
Unifactorial (Mendelian) Autosomal Recessive Disorder.
- Specifically Thalassemia or Sickle Cell Anemia.
- Manifests after 6 months of age as HbF levels decline.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Explain the diagnostic mechanism and clinical utility of measuring alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) in amniotic fluid at 14–16 weeks of gestation.
back:
Detects Neural Tube Defects (NTDs).
- Elevated AFP indicates leakage from fetal neural tissues.
- Used to diagnose anencephaly and spina bifida via amniocentesis.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Contrast the inheritance and environmental characteristics of Mendelian diseases with those of Multifactorial disorders like Essential Hypertension.
back:
- Mendelian: Single gene mutation, follows fixed laws (1:4 or 1:2 risk), minimal environmental impact.
- Multifactorial: Polygenic, lacks clear pedigree patterns, heavily influenced by environment (diet, stress).

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Differentiate between Prospective and Retrospective Genetic Counseling strategies used in community health programs.
back:
- Prospective: Screening healthy carriers (heterozygotes) before marriage or conception to prevent the first occurrence.
- Retrospective: Counseling provided after an affected child is already born into a family.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Genetic disorders resulting from the interaction of multiple genes and environmental factors, such as essential hypertension and diabetes mellitus, are classified as [___] disorders.
back:
• Multifactorial disorders.
• Most common genetic group in adult populations.
• Influence of lifestyle/environment (diet, exercise) is significant.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A 42-year-old pregnant female is concerned about fetal chromosomal anomalies. The most common numerical autosomal abnormality associated with advanced maternal age is [___].
back:
• Down’s Syndrome (Trisomy 21).
• Caused by meiotic non-disjunction.
• Risk at age 45 is 1 in 50 births.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Explain the inheritance risk for offspring when both parents are heterozygous carriers of an autosomal recessive trait like Phenylketonuria (PKU).
back:
• 25% chance of being affected (homozygous).
• 50% chance of being healthy carriers (heterozygous).
• 25% chance of being genetically normal.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Contrast the chromosomal constitution and primary clinical features of Klinefelter’s Syndrome versus Turner’s Syndrome.
back:
• Klinefelter: 47,XXY; eunuchoid male, gynaecomastia, non-functional testes.
• Turner: 45,XO; short stature female, primary amenorrhoea, webbed neck.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Identify the transmission pattern where a mutant gene on the X-chromosome is passed from an affected father to all his daughters, making them carriers, while all his sons remain unaffected.
back:
• X-linked recessive inheritance.
• Examples: Haemophilia, Colour blindness, G6PD deficiency.
• Males are more commonly affected as they lack a second X-allele.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: The primary preventive measure involving the identification of heterozygous carriers before marriage or conception to avoid births of affected individuals is [___] genetic counseling.
back:
• Prospective genetic counseling.
• Utilizes community screening (e.g., Thalassemia screening).
• Aims for true primary prevention.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A couple belonging to a community with high rates of first-cousin marriages presents for counseling. This practice increases the offspring's risk of [___] disorders.
back:
• Autosomal recessive disorders.
• Consanguinity increases the probability of matching rare recessive alleles.
• Examples: Alkaptonuria, PKU, Albinism.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Describe the utility of Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) testing in prenatal diagnosis via maternal serum or amniotic fluid.
back:
• Elevated levels indicate Neural Tube Defects (Anencephaly, Spina Bifida).
• Decreased levels may suggest Down's Syndrome.
• Used for widespread community screening.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Contrast the preventive objectives of Negative Eugenics with Euthenics.
back:
• Negative Eugenics: Reducing frequencies of harmful genes by discouraging/preventing procreation of defectives.
• Euthenics: Improving the phenotype through environmental manipulation (e.g., diet, education).

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Name the law stating that relative frequencies of gene alleles remain constant from generation to generation in a large, randomly mating population.
back:
• Hardy-Weinberg Law.
• Central theme of population genetics.
• Influenced by mutation, natural selection, and population migration.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A numerical chromosomal abnormality where the chromosome number is not an exact multiple of the haploid set is termed [___].
back:
• Aneuploidy.
• Includes trisomy (extra chromosome) or monosomy (missing chromosome).
• Commonly results from non-disjunction during cell division.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A child presents with short stature, tilted eye-slits, a small round head, and mental retardation. Karyotyping reveals an extra chromosome on the 21st pair. Identify the condition and its primary risk factor.
back:
• Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21).
• Primary risk factor is advanced maternal age (e.g., 1 in 50 risk at age 45).
• Associated with cardiac and alimentary tract defects.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Explain the biological mechanism of non-disjunction as it relates to the development of numerical chromosomal disorders.
back:
• Failure of homologous chromosomes or chromatids to separate during meiosis.
• Results in gametes with extra or missing chromosomes.
• Fertilization leads to conditions like Klinefelter (XXY) or Turner (XO) syndromes.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Contrast the inheritance patterns of autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive traits regarding parentage and risk of occurrence in offspring.
back:
• Dominant: Expressed in heterozygotes; 50% risk if one parent is affected.
• Recessive: Expressed only in homozygotes; 25% risk if both parents are carriers.
• Dominant traits appear vertically; recessive traits appear sporadically.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Define the specific aim and methodology associated with Negative Eugenics in community health.
back:
• Aim: Reduce the frequency of hereditary diseases in the community.
• Methods: Sterilization or debarring affected individuals from procreating.
• Focuses on preventing transmission of serious genetic defects.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: The autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a deficiency of the liver enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase is [___].
back:
• Phenylketonuria (PKU).
• Leads to accumulation of phenylalanine, which is toxic to the brain.
• Results in mental retardation if not managed by diet.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: An adult male presents with eunuchoid features, gynaecomastia, non-functional testes, and azoospermia. Karyotype reveals 47, XXY. State the clinical diagnosis.
back:
• Klinefelter’s Syndrome.
• Most common sex-chromosome aneuploidy in males.
• Features include scanty body hair and mental retardation.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Describe how environmental factors interact with genetic predisposition in the aetiology of multifactorial disorders.
back:
• Polygenic inheritance interacts with external triggers.
• Environmental triggers: diet, obesity, smoking, and lack of exercise.
• Common examples: Diabetes mellitus, essential hypertension, and ischaemic heart disease.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Distinguish between Genotype and Phenotype in the context of human genetic expression.
back:
• Genotype: The total genetic constitution (fixed; e.g., genetic code for blood group).
• Phenotype: The outward, plastic expression (e.g., physical appearance, stature).
• Medicine is often the management of the human phenotype.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Identify the standard timing and diagnostic utility of amniocentesis in community prenatal screening.
back:
• Timing: Between 14–16 weeks of pregnancy.
• Utility: Detects chromosomal anomalies (Down’s) and neural tube defects.
• Involves biochemical analysis and karyotyping of fetal cells.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: The most common autosomal trisomy in the community, characterized by short stature and mental retardation, whose frequency increases significantly with maternal age is [___].
back:
Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21)
- Risk increases sharply after maternal age of 35.
- Incidence is approximately 1 in 900 births.
- Clinical features include flat facies and cardiac defects.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A child in a Pakistani community presents with severe anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and 'chipmunk facies' on X-ray. Both parents are healthy but have a family history of blood disorders. Identify the likely inheritance pattern.
back:
Autosomal Recessive (Thalassemia Major)
- High prevalence in Pakistan due to consanguineous marriages.
- Results from reduced synthesis of globin chains.
- Requires both parents to be heterozygous carriers.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Explain the role of environmental factors in the expression of multifactorial disorders like Diabetes Mellitus and Hypertension.
back:
Heredity-Environment Interaction:
- Polygenic inheritance provides the genetic susceptibility.
- Environmental triggers (obesity, sedentary lifestyle, diet) unmask the disease.
- The disorder manifests only when the threshold of liability is exceeded.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Contrast Turner Syndrome and Klinefelter Syndrome regarding their chromosomal constitution and phenotypic gender.
back:
Turner Syndrome:
- 45, XO constitution.
- Phenotypic female; short stature, webbed neck, infertile.
Klinefelter Syndrome:
- 47, XXY constitution.
- Phenotypic male; gynaecomastia, small firm testes, azoospermia.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Describe the transmission pattern of X-linked recessive disorders, such as Haemophilia A, from an affected father.
back:
Criss-Cross Inheritance:
- Affected fathers transmit the gene to all daughters (carriers).
- Affected fathers transmit no genes to their sons.
- Disease typically skips generations, manifesting primarily in males.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: For the prenatal diagnosis of chromosomal anomalies and neural tube defects, the sampling procedure typically performed between the 14th and 16th weeks of pregnancy is [___].
back:
Amniocentesis
- Karyotyping detects trisomies (Down Syndrome).
- Elevated Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) indicates neural tube defects.
- Allows for biochemical analysis of inborn errors of metabolism.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: A population study finds a high frequency of the Sickle Cell gene (HbS) in malaria-endemic regions despite its lethal effect in homozygotes. Explain this phenomenon.
back:
Heterozygote Advantage (Balanced Polymorphism):
- Carriers (HbAS) are resistant to Falciparum malaria.
- Natural selection preserves the gene in the pool for survival.
- Homozygotes (HbSS) suffer severe hemolytic anemia.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Explain why consanguineous marriages are a major public health concern regarding the incidence of rare metabolic disorders.
back:
Increased Homozygosity:
- High risk of hidden recessive genes meeting in offspring.
- Elevates incidence of conditions like PKU, Albinism, and Thalassemia.
- Offspring have higher premature death rates compared to non-consanguineous groups.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: Distinguish between the terms 'Genotype' and 'Phenotype' in the management of genetic diseases.
back:
Genotype:
- The fixed genetic constitution (e.g., DNA sequence).
Phenotype:
- The plastic, outward expression of genes (e.g., physical traits).
- Medicine focuses on managing the phenotype to improve health despite fixed genotypes.

category: Classify types of genetic disorders common in community
front: List the three primary clinical classifications of genetic disorders found in the community.
back:
1. Chromosomal Abnormalities (e.g., Aneuploidy).
2. Unifactorial/Mendelian Diseases (Single-gene: Dominant, Recessive, X-linked).
3. Multifactorial Disorders (Polygenic + Environment: e.g., IHD, DM).

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: The science that aims to reduce the frequency of hereditary disabilities in a community by debarring affected individuals from producing children is known as [___].
back:
• Negative Eugenics
• Focuses on reducing harmful gene frequency
• Utilizes measures like sterilization or contraception
• Aims to minimize genetic burden in the population

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: A couple, both identified as carriers of the Beta-thalassemia trait through premarital screening, seeks advice to avoid having an affected child. This preventive approach is [___].
back:
• Prospective Genetic Counselling
• Identifies heterozygous individuals before marriage
• Prevents the birth of affected children
• Targets high-risk recessive traits like Thalassemia or Sickle Cell

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Explain the role of amniocentesis in the early diagnosis of genetic disorders.
back:
• Performed at 14–16 weeks gestation
• Fetal cells are karyotyped for chromosomal anomalies (e.g., Down Syndrome)
• Biochemical analysis detects inborn errors of metabolism
• Alpha-fetoprotein levels screen for neural tube defects

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Contrast the objectives of negative eugenics with those of positive eugenics.
back:
• Negative: Eliminates defects by debarring weak/defective carriers
• Positive: Encourages carriers of desirable genotypes to reproduce
• Negative focus: Sterilization/Contraception
• Positive focus: Complex multifactorial traits (e.g., intelligence)

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Detail why avoiding consanguineous marriages is a key health promotional measure for genetic health.
back:
• Reduces risk of autosomal recessive traits (e.g., PKU, Albinism)
• Minimizes the frequency of polygenic disorders
• Lowers the risk of premature death in offspring
• Prevents the pairing of hidden heterozygous carriers

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: The science of improving the human race by manipulating the environment to allow genes to express their full potential (e.g., environmental stimulation for IQ) is [___].
back:
• Euthenics
• Focuses on environmental manipulation rather than genotype change
• Involves nutrition, education, and stimulation
• Based on the interaction between nature and nurture

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: A 45-year-old pregnant woman carries a 1 in 50 risk of having a child with Down Syndrome. Specify the primary health promotional recommendation regarding marriage/childbearing age to prevent this.
back:
• Promotion of early marriage/childbearing (ideally <35 years)
• Incidence of Trisomy 21 rises steeply with maternal age
• Risk at age 20 is only 1:3000
• Encourages reproduction during optimal biological window

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Explain the biological necessity for timing the Guthrie test 48 hours to 7 days after birth in neonates.
back:
• Detects Phenylketonuria (PKU)
• Requires infant to ingest protein/formula first
• Phenylalanine levels must build up post-feeding to be detectable
• Prevents false negatives in early neonatal screening

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Contrast the clinical context of prospective vs. retrospective genetic counselling.
back:
• Prospective: True prevention; identifying carriers before they have an affected child
• Retrospective: Occurs after a family member is already affected
• Prospective uses: Premarital screening
• Retrospective uses: Contraception, sterilization, or pregnancy termination advice

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: List specific protection measures to guard the community against environmental mutagens.
back:
• Lead shielding of gonads during X-ray procedures
• Avoiding unnecessary X-rays during pregnancy
• Controlling exposure to chemical mutagens/carcinogens
• Monitoring ionizing radiation in occupational settings

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: The science which aims to improve the genetic endowment of a human population through measures like debarring the marriage of individuals with serious hereditary diseases is termed [___].
back: Negative Eugenics. • Aims to reduce the frequency of hereditary disabilities. • Achieved by discouraging procreation in individuals with serious defects. • Lessens the overall genetic burden on the community.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: A couple in a high-prevalence area for Beta-Thalassemia undergoes screening to identify their carrier status before marriage. This type of health promotional measure is known as [___].
back: Prospective Genetic Counseling. • Allows for true prevention before a child is born. • Identifies heterozygous carriers for recessive defects. • Explains marriage risks to prevent affected offspring.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Explain the biological rationale behind 'Euthenics' as a health promotional measure for genetic health.
back: Environmental manipulation to maximize genetic expression. • Genes require a suitable environment to manifest potential. • Examples include nutritional intervention and environmental stimulation. • Complements eugenic measures.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Contrast the primary objective of prospective genetic counseling with that of retrospective genetic counseling.
back: • Prospective: Prevents first occurrence by screening carriers before marriage. • Retrospective: Advice given after an affected child is born. • Retrospective uses contraception, termination, or sterilization.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Identify the primary genetic risk and specific disease examples associated with consanguineous marriages in a community.
back: Increased risk of autosomal recessive traits. • Related parents are likely to carry the same recessive gene. • Examples: Albinism, Phenylketonuria (PKU), and Alkaptonuria.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: The risk of Trisomy 21 (Down’s Syndrome) increases significantly with [___], making early marriage a key health promotional recommendation.
back: Advanced Maternal Age. • Risk at age 20 is approximately 1:3000. • Risk rises to 1:50 by age 45. • Unaffected by paternal age.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: A 38-year-old pregnant woman seeks prenatal diagnosis for chromosomal anomalies. The gold-standard procedure typically performed between 14–16 weeks is [___].
back: Amniocentesis. • Karyotyping of fetal cells from amniotic fluid. • Detects chromosomal anomalies (Down's) and metabolic defects. • Fetal cells are cultured for biochemical analysis.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: How does 'Specific Protection' serve as a preventive measure against the emergence of new genetic mutations in a population?
back: Protection against environmental mutagens. • Shielding gonads during medical X-rays. • Avoiding ionizing radiation and chemical mutagens. • Prevents point mutations and chromosomal damage.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Distinguish between positive eugenics and negative eugenics as health promotional tools.
back: • Positive: Encourages procreation among carriers of desirable genotypes (limited application). • Negative: Prevents procreation in those with serious hereditary disease. • Negative eugenics is more practical.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Name the specific protective intervention used to prevent Rh-haemolytic disease in the newborn of an Rh-negative mother.
back: Anti-D Globulin (Immunization). • Prevents maternal antibody production against Rh-positive cells. • Administered to Rh-negative mothers. • Controls genetically determined immunological disorders.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: The branch of eugenics that aims to improve the genetic composition of a population by encouraging individuals with desirable genotypes to reproduce is known as [___] eugenics.
back:
• Positive Eugenics
• Encourages carriers of socially valuable traits to assume parenthood
• Difficult to implement due to complex, multifactorial determination of most traits.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: A couple, both known carriers of the Beta-thalassemia trait, seeks medical advice before marriage. Identify the specific type of genetic counselling required in this pre-conception stage.
back:
• Prospective Genetic Counselling
• Involves identifying heterozygous carriers via screening procedures
• Focuses on explaining risks to prevent the first occurrence of the disease.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Explain how 'Euthenics' acts as a health promotional measure for genetic health.
back:
• Environmental manipulation to improve phenotypic expression
• Providing access to optimal nutrition, stimulation, and surroundings
• Ensures existing genotypes (like intelligence) reach their full potential.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Contrast the primary methods used in Negative Eugenics versus Positive Eugenics.
back:
• Negative: Reduces hereditary disability by discouraging reproduction (e.g., sterilization or debarring) of affected individuals
• Positive: Enhances population quality by encouraging reproduction of superior genotypes.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: List the high-yield maternal lifestyle and health promotional recommendations to prevent chromosomal trisomies like Down's Syndrome.
back:
• Avoiding late marriages and delayed childbearing (ideally before age 35)
• Prenatal screening (amniocentesis) for high-risk age groups
• Awareness that risk rises from 1:3000 at age 20 to 1:50 at age 45.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: The health promotional measure involving the discouragement of [___] marriages is essential to reduce the frequency of autosomal recessive disorders like Albinism and PKU.
back:
• Consanguineous (Blood-relative) marriages
• Increases the probability of offspring inheriting identical recessive genes from a common ancestor
• Linked to higher premature death rates.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: A mother who previously gave birth to a child with anencephaly seeks advice for her next pregnancy. Identify the appropriate retrospective measures for her.
back:
• Retrospective Genetic Counselling
• Prenatal diagnosis via Alpha-fetoprotein levels and amniocentesis
• Specific protection through periconceptional folic acid supplementation.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Describe the 'Specific Protection' mechanism used to prevent Rh-haemolytic disease of the newborn.
back:
• Immunization with Anti-D Globulin
• Administered to Rh-negative mothers post-exposure
• Prevents maternal sensitization against fetal Rh-positive red cells.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Contrast the utility of Prospective versus Retrospective Genetic Counselling.
back:
• Prospective: True prevention identifying carriers before they have an affected child
• Retrospective: Advice given after a disorder has already occurred in the family.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Identify the primary environmental mutagens against which communities require 'Specific Protection' to maintain genetic integrity.
back:
• Ionizing radiation (unnecessary X-ray exposure, especially of gonads/pregnant uterus)
• Chemical mutagens (carcinogens)
• Ultraviolet rays.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Environmental manipulation aimed at providing an improved genotype with the best possible surroundings for gene expression is termed [___].
back: * Euthenics. * Focuses on optimizing environmental factors like nutrition and stimulation. * Enables genes to reach their full biological potential. * Complements rather than replaces genetic improvement.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: A couple who recently had a child born with Thalassemia Major seeks medical advice regarding the risks for future pregnancies. This form of health promotion is classified as [___] genetic counseling.
back: * Retrospective genetic counseling. * Initiated after a hereditary disorder is already identified in a family. * Methods include contraception, pregnancy termination, or sterilization. * Aims to prevent the recurrence of the disorder.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Explain the operational mechanism and primary goal of prospective genetic counseling in community health management.
back: * Mechanism: Identifies heterozygous (carrier) individuals through population-wide screening procedures. * Goal: Educates carriers on risks of marrying other heterozygotes for the same gene. * Outcome: True prevention by reducing births of affected children.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
front: Contrast the fundamental objectives of negative eugenics with those of positive eugenics in the context of improving a population's genetic endowment.
back: * Negative Eugenics: Aims to reduce frequency of defects by debarring affected individuals or carriers from reproduction. * Positive Eugenics: Encourages individuals with desirable, socially valuable genotypes to assume the burden of parenthood. * Contrast: Negative focuses on elimination; Positive focuses on enhancement.

category: Describe health promotional measures to control genetic diseases
